items.title: Ukraine wants to use AI to predict where Russian drones will hit the battlefield with 'high probability'
items.summary: A soldier from the Striletskyi special forces police battalion of the National Police in the Zaporizhzhia region looks at a smartphone near a Ukrainian 2S22 Bohdana 155 mm self-propelled howitzer. Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images Ukraine says it's about to start using an AI model that can forecast drone threats on the front lines. It said the tool analyzes battlefield data to predict how, where, and when Russia will strike. The model, dubbed No. 13, was jointly developed with NATO, its defense ministry said. Ukraine's defense ministry said on Tuesday that its forces are about to start using a jointly NATO-developed artificial intelligence model to predict where and when Russia's drone strikes will land. Dubbed "Model No. 13," the tool analyzes past combat data, weather conditions, and battlefield conditions to determine, with "high probability," how Russian troops will use drones on the front lines, the ministry said in a statement. The model can forecast the strike's time, location, intensity, and type of drone used, the ministry said. "The solution has already been validated using real-world datasets. It has been refined and is ready for integration into the Armed Forces of Ukraine's situational awareness systems," its statement read. The ministry said Model No. 13 was developed by its armed forces and NATO's Allied Command Transformation , with support from the Joint Analysis, Training and Education Center, an organization the alliance created in late 2024 to help it innovate based on lessons learned in the war. ACT and JATEC did not immediately respond to requests for comment sent outside regular business hours by Business Insider. Another AI model that plans artillery deployments, No. 32, is also being jointly created, Ukraine's defense ministry said. However, Ukrainian troops are still testing a prototype of the model, it added. The announcement comes after Ukrainian officials said in February that their forces had been working with AI and machine learning models since last year to process combat data from the war for "threat forecasting." Model No. 13 is likely to run on Ukraine's DELTA battlefield management system , a digital app that combines intelligence from drones, cameras, and battlefield reports to give commanders an overview of the frontline from their tablets or phones. The system already uses an AI module called Vezha that Ukraine says can automatically detect and flag Russian equipment in seconds by analyzing satellite imagery, drone camera feeds, and radio signals. DELTA reached over 200,000 users in November, Ukraine's defense ministry has said. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Stop Writing _ => throw for Cases That Can't Happen. C# 15 Has Unions
items.summary: TL;DR: C# 15 adds union types: union LookupResult(Found, NotFound, Invalid); . Assign any case type, switch over it, and the compiler checks you handled every case. It ships with .NET 11, which is at Release Candidate 1 right now: go-live licensed, but not final yet. The arm that says "unreachable, promise" You have a method that can end three ways. You want callers to handle all three. So you reach for the classic C# workaround: a marker interface. ILookupResult result = new Discontinued ( "OLD-1" ); string message = result switch { Found f => $" { f . Sku } : { f . Stock } in stock" , NotFound n => $" { n . Sku } : no such product" , Invalid i => $"rejected: { i . Reason } " , _ => throw new InvalidOperationException ( "unreachable, promise" ), }; interface ILookupResult ; record Found ( string Sku , int Stock ) : ILookupResult ; record NotFound ( string Sku ) : ILookupResult ; record Invalid ( string Reason ) : ILookupResult ; record Discontinued ( string Sku ) : ILookupResult ; The compiler cannot know that only three types implement the interface. So it demands the _ arm, and you write a throw for a case that "can't happen". Then a teammate adds Discontinued . Everything compiles. When I ran it, the result was Unhandled exception. System.InvalidOperationException: unreachable, promise . The promise lasted exactly one pull request. Meet union types A union names a closed set of types. A value of the union is exactly one of them: record Dog ( string Name ); record Cat ( string Name ); union Pet ( Cat , Dog ); Any case type converts to the union implicitly, and pattern matching looks straight through it: Pet pet = new Dog ( "Rex" ); string name = pet switch { Dog d => $"dog { d . Name } " , Cat c => $"cat { c . Name } " , }; Console . WriteLine ( name ); // dog Rex Console . WriteLine ( pet . Value ); // Dog { Name = Rex } No _ arm, and no warning. Sku } : { f . Stock } in stock" , NotFound n => $" { n . Sku } : no such product" , Invalid i => $"rejected: { i . Reason } " , }; Console . WriteLine ( message ); } static LookupResult Lookup ( string sku ) { if ( string . IsNullOrWhiteSpace ( sku )) return new Invalid ( "SKU is empty" ); if (! sku . Contains ( '-' )) return new Invalid ( $"' { sku } ' has no dash" ); return sku switch { "ABC-123" => new Found ( sku , 12 ), "XYZ-9" => new Found ( sku , 0 ), _ => new NotFound ( sku ), }; } record Found ( string Sku , int Stock ); record NotFound ( string Sku ); record Invalid ( string Reason ); union LookupResult ( Found , NotFound , Invalid ); Output from the run: ABC-123: 12 in stock rejected: SKU is empty XYZ-9: 0 in stock QQQ-404: no such product Each return hands back a plain record, and the union conversion does the rest. WriteLine ( Show ( legacy )); // legacy #1234 Console . WriteLine ( Show ( modern )); // user 3f2b8c1e000040008000000000000001 static string Show ( UserId id ) => id switch { int n => $"legacy # { n } " , Guid g => $"user { g : N } " , }; union UserId ( int , Guid ); Try doing that with a marker interface. int will not sign up. Can I use it? Union types are part of C# 15. On the .NET 11 RC1 SDK, #error version reports Language version: 15.0 , and every snippet here compiled with no LangVersion set. The UnionAttribute and IUnion types the compiler relies on are in the runtime starting with .NET 11 Preview 5. .NET 11 RC1 shipped on September 8, 2026 with a go-live support license, so it is allowed in production. It is still a release candidate, though, not the final release. Microsoft's docs note that some parts of the union proposal are not implemented yet and are coming later. On the .NET 10 SDK (C# 14), union is not a keyword at all, and the same file fails with syntax errors such as CS1001: Identifier expected . I ran every snippet here as a file-based app with dotnet run file.cs on SDK 11.0.100-rc.1. Gotchas 1. A union is a struct, and it holds an object? . The compiler turns union Pet(Cat, Dog) into a struct with one Value property of type object? . Unsafe.SizeOf () printed 8 in my run: one reference, nothing more. 2. Value-type cases get boxed. Because Value is an object? , an int case is boxed on the way in. Storing 1,000 int values in a UserId allocated 24,000 bytes in my test, 24 bytes each. For hot paths, the docs show how to write a custom union with TryGetValue members that avoid the box. 3. default is a union with nothing inside. Pet nobody = default; has a Value of null . In my test, switching over it with only the Dog and Cat arms compiled with no warning and then threw SwitchExpressionException at runtime. If a union can come from default , an uninitialized field, or an array slot, add a null arm. 4. Its sibling is closed . If your cases already share a base class, C# 15 also has the closed modifier, which limits derived classes to the same assembly and gives you the same exhaustive switch . Use union when the cases have nothing in common, and closed when they do. Wrap-up A _ => throw arm is a comment that crashes. A union turns it into a compiler warning on the day the new case lands, which is the cheapest day to find it. Go find the "unreachable" exception in your codebase and see if it is really a union in disguise. items.summary_html:
TL;DR: C# 15 adds union types: union LookupResult(Found, NotFound, Invalid);. Assign any case type, switch over it, and the compiler checks you handled every case. It ships with .NET 11, which is at Release Candidate 1 right now: go-live licensed, but not final yet.

The arm that says "unreachable, promise"

You have a method that can end three ways. You want callers to handle all three. So you reach for the classic C# workaround: a marker interface.

ILookupResult result = new Discontinued("OLD-1");

string message = result switch
{
    Found f => $"{f.Sku}: {f.Stock} in stock",
    NotFound n => $"{n.Sku}: no such product",
    Invalid i => $"rejected: {i.Reason}",
    _ => throw new InvalidOperationException("unreachable, promise"),
};

interface ILookupResult;
record Found(string Sku, int Stock) : ILookupResult;
record NotFound(string Sku) : ILookupResult;
record Invalid(string Reason) : ILookupResult;
record Discontinued(string Sku) : ILookupResult;

The compiler cannot know that only three types implement the interface. So it demands the _ arm, and you write a throw for a case that "can't happen".

Then a teammate adds Discontinued. Everything compiles. When I ran it, the result was Unhandled exception. System.InvalidOperationException: unreachable, promise. The promise lasted exactly one pull request.

Meet union types

A union names a closed set of types. A value of the union is exactly one of them:

record Dog(string Name);
record Cat(string Name);

union Pet(Cat, Dog);

Any case type converts to the union implicitly, and pattern matching looks straight through it:

Pet pet = new Dog("Rex");

string name = pet switch
{
    Dog d => $"dog {d.Name}",
    Cat c => $"cat {c.Name}",
};

Console.WriteLine(name);      // dog Rex
Console.WriteLine(pet.Value); // Dog { Name = Rex }

No _ arm, and no warning. The compiler knows Cat and Dog are the whole list.

Assigning anything else is a compile error: Pet p = "a string"; gives CS0029: Cannot implicitly convert type 'string' to 'Pet'.

The case types do not need a shared base class or interface. They do not even need to be yours.

A realistic one: a product lookup

Here is the same lookup from the top, as a union:

string[] inputs = ["ABC-123", "", "XYZ-9", "QQQ-404"];

foreach (var input in inputs)
{
    LookupResult result = Lookup(input);

    string message = result switch
    {
        Found f => $"{f.Sku}: {f.Stock} in stock",
        NotFound n => $"{n.Sku}: no such product",
        Invalid i => $"rejected: {i.Reason}",
    };

    Console.WriteLine(message);
}

static LookupResult Lookup(string sku)
{
    if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(sku))
        return new Invalid("SKU is empty");

    if (!sku.Contains('-'))
        return new Invalid($"'{sku}' has no dash");

    return sku switch
    {
        "ABC-123" => new Found(sku, 12),
        "XYZ-9" => new Found(sku, 0),
        _ => new NotFound(sku),
    };
}

record Found(string Sku, int Stock);
record NotFound(string Sku);
record Invalid(string Reason);

union LookupResult(Found, NotFound, Invalid);

Output from the run:

ABC-123: 12 in stock
rejected: SKU is empty
XYZ-9: 0 in stock
QQQ-404: no such product

Each return hands back a plain record, and the union conversion does the rest.

Now the teammate adds Discontinued to the union. This time the build tells on them:

warning CS8509: The switch expression does not handle all possible values of its input type (it is not exhaustive). For example, the pattern 'Discontinued' is not covered.

That warning shows up at every switch that missed the new case. With TreatWarningsAsErrors on, it is a failed build instead of a 2 AM page.

Types you don't own

Because a union does not need inheritance, it can mix types you could never give a common base. Say your old users have int ids and new users have Guid ids:

UserId legacy = 1234;
UserId modern = Guid.Parse("3f2b8c1e-0000-4000-8000-000000000001");

Console.WriteLine(Show(legacy)); // legacy #1234
Console.WriteLine(Show(modern)); // user 3f2b8c1e000040008000000000000001

static string Show(UserId id) => id switch
{
    int n => $"legacy #{n}",
    Guid g => $"user {g:N}",
};

union UserId(int, Guid);

Try doing that with a marker interface. int will not sign up.

Can I use it?
  • Union types are part of C# 15. On the .NET 11 RC1 SDK, #error version reports Language version: 15.0, and every snippet here compiled with no LangVersion set.
  • The UnionAttribute and IUnion types the compiler relies on are in the runtime starting with .NET 11 Preview 5.
  • .NET 11 RC1 shipped on September 8, 2026 with a go-live support license, so it is allowed in production. It is still a release candidate, though, not the final release.
  • Microsoft's docs note that some parts of the union proposal are not implemented yet and are coming later.
  • On the .NET 10 SDK (C# 14), union is not a keyword at all, and the same file fails with syntax errors such as CS1001: Identifier expected.

I ran every snippet here as a file-based app with dotnet run file.cs on SDK 11.0.100-rc.1.

Gotchas

1. A union is a struct, and it holds an object?. The compiler turns union Pet(Cat, Dog) into a struct with one Value property of type object?. Unsafe.SizeOf() printed 8 in my run: one reference, nothing more.

2. Value-type cases get boxed. Because Value is an object?, an int case is boxed on the way in. Storing 1,000 int values in a UserId allocated 24,000 bytes in my test, 24 bytes each. For hot paths, the docs show how to write a custom union with TryGetValue members that avoid the box.

3. default is a union with nothing inside. Pet nobody = default; has a Value of null. In my test, switching over it with only the Dog and Cat arms compiled with no warning and then threw SwitchExpressionException at runtime. If a union can come from default, an uninitialized field, or an array slot, add a null arm.

4. Its sibling is closed. If your cases already share a base class, C# 15 also has the closed modifier, which limits derived classes to the same assembly and gives you the same exhaustive switch. Use union when the cases have nothing in common, and closed when they do.

Wrap-up

A _ => throw arm is a comment that crashes. A union turns it into a compiler warning on the day the new case lands, which is the cheapest day to find it. Go find the "unreachable" exception in your codebase and see if it is really a union in disguise.

  • Union types, C# reference (Microsoft Learn)
  • Feature specification: Unions
  • The closed modifier (Microsoft Learn)
  • Announcing .NET 11 Release Candidate 1 (.NET Blog)

items.title: Modeling a Cushing Tank Farm: A Map-to-3D Workflow and Its Validation Checks
items.summary: When I model an industrial site, I want to separate three things that can look identical on screen: verified data, contextual data, and generated content. Cushing, Oklahoma, is a useful example because the crude oil storage landscape includes many repeated tanks, connecting pipeline corridors, roads, pump equipment, and wider transportation links. A detailed render can make those elements feel equally certain, even when they come from very different sources. I would build an early Cushing scene to answer a bounded question: how does one selected area of the tank district relate to nearby roads and transport infrastructure? I would not use a generated scene to estimate capacity, identify active lines, or make an operational decision. 1. Define the extent before generating geometry I start by choosing a map boundary that includes the tank groups relevant to the question, plus enough surrounding land to show access and connections. A boundary that is too tight turns the model into a collection of objects with no context. One that is too broad may make the storage layout hard to inspect. I record the selected extent and the reason for choosing it so another reviewer can reproduce the view. Shapezo can support this first pass: I select an area on a map, and its AI generates a model of that place. That gives me a fast spatial draft for discussion. I would record that it is generated context, along with its creation date and any known limitations, before bringing it into a technical review. 2. Separate scene layers by confidence I would keep tank footprints, roads, rail, pipelines, buildings, and open land in distinct layers. If some features come from trusted mapping and others are inferred, they should not share the same visual status. A simple legend or metadata field can distinguish verified geometry from illustrative geometry. This matters because repetition creates false confidence: dozens of similar tanks can make an approximate layout look like an inventory. The geometry should be fit for its intended question. A broad overview may need only the location and spacing of tank groups. A maintenance access review would need better information about roads, gates, working clearances, and internal circulation. The model should not pretend to support a level of analysis its source data cannot handle. 3. Validate the spatial relationships Before I use the scene, I check coordinate reference, scale, orientation, and terrain context. Then I compare recognizable features such as road intersections, rail alignments, and facility edges with dependable mapping. I look for misplaced or duplicate geometry, especially where the AI may have regularized repeated objects. If the pipeline layer is not authoritative, I do not label a line as an actual active route. For an early visualization, this can be a lightweight review. For engineering, safety, or regulatory work, it is not enough. Those uses need source records, professional review, and more precise data. The distinction belongs in the file itself so it survives handoff. 4. Add the operational scene carefully A useful tank-farm view can include containment areas, pumps, pipe corridors, access routes, rail sidings, and maintenance zones. I add these details only at the level supported by the available information. For example, I can create a generic inspection scene with platforms and coating equipment, but I should not imply that a named tank is under repair or that a particular procedure is being followed. This is also where environmental context belongs. Drainage paths, perimeter vegetation, and adjacent land uses influence how a site meets its surroundings. A generated image cannot establish runoff performance or spill protection. It can show why those questions matter and which records might answer them. 5. Preserve provenance at export When I share a model, I include the map extent, source dates, coordinate system, layer status, and intended use. I keep the Shapezo output separate from any authoritative facility data. If someone exports a scene to another tool, the metadata should travel with it or be attached in a short manifest. A screenshot without provenance is easy to misread. My practical rule I use Shapezo to create a first spatial draft from a selected map area. I use verified data to check geometry and to support any claim that affects operations or design. Cushing’s tank farms make that separation especially visible: the scene has many repeated assets, but a visually complete model is not the same as a dependable asset register. The workflow is useful when it speeds up orientation without blurring that boundary.

items.title: RD-AGENT 第六讲 · 一次预注册实验的完整生命周期：两份判决书
items.summary: 第六讲 · 一次预注册实验的完整生命周期：两份判决书 第二章 · 诚实的验证（第三讲，本章收尾） 学习目标：跟踪两个真实假设从立项到判决的全过程，掌握预注册实验的操作细节与三种判决的分界。 前置：第四、五讲。 1. 为什么选这两个案例 第五讲的全 FAIL 是"批量候选"的结局；本讲看 单个假设的完整生命周期 ——人提出想法、写成预注册、走完验证、拿到判决、执行判决后果。两个案例一个 REJECTED、一个 INCONCLUSIVE，正好覆盖"否决后怎么办"和"证据不足时怎么办"这两个最难的操作。（SUPPORTED 的案例留给第四章，避免结构上"大团圆"得太早。） 2. 案例一：业绩预告事件窗 —— REJECTED 2.1 假设 A 股业绩预告披露前后存在可交易的定价偏差窗口：预告超预期的股票在事件后若干日仍有漂移（盈余公告后漂移，PEAD 的预告版）。数据基础：业绩预告数据（forecast）+ 曾用名变更（namechange）面板。 2.2 预注册要点 判决前锁定的要素（节选）：事件窗定义、对照组构造、OOS 窗口、价差门槛（方向 + 量级 + 显著性）、以及三种判决的边界。 在触碰任何 OOS 数据之前完成存档。 2.3 判决 OOS 价差 −0.49%，方向反。REJECTED，一次判定。 发现期（IS 段）同样没有可用的正价差——这个细节很重要：它不是"发现期有效、样本外翻车"的经典过拟合形态，而是 从头到尾就不存在 。假设本身错了，不是数据 unlucky。 2.4 判决的执行——最见制度成色的部分 REJECTED 落地后发生了三件事，每件都值得讲： 假设族封禁 第六讲 · 一次预注册实验的完整生命周期：两份判决书

第二章 · 诚实的验证（第三讲，本章收尾）
学习目标：跟踪两个真实假设从立项到判决的全过程，掌握预注册实验的操作细节与三种判决的分界。
前置：第四、五讲。

1. 为什么选这两个案例

第五讲的全 FAIL 是"批量候选"的结局；本讲看单个假设的完整生命周期——人提出想法、写成预注册、走完验证、拿到判决、执行判决后果。两个案例一个 REJECTED、一个 INCONCLUSIVE，正好覆盖"否决后怎么办"和"证据不足时怎么办"这两个最难的操作。（SUPPORTED 的案例留给第四章，避免结构上"大团圆"得太早。）

2. 案例一：业绩预告事件窗 —— REJECTED 2.1 假设

A 股业绩预告披露前后存在可交易的定价偏差窗口：预告超预期的股票在事件后若干日仍有漂移（盈余公告后漂移，PEAD 的预告版）。数据基础：业绩预告数据（forecast）+ 曾用名变更（namechange）面板。

2.2 预注册要点

判决前锁定的要素（节选）：事件窗定义、对照组构造、OOS 窗口、价差门槛（方向 + 量级 + 显著性）、以及三种判决的边界。在触碰任何 OOS 数据之前完成存档。

2.3 判决

OOS 价差 −0.49%，方向反。REJECTED，一次判定。

发现期（IS 段）同样没有可用的正价差——这个细节很重要：它不是"发现期有效、样本外翻车"的经典过拟合形态，而是从头到尾就不存在。假设本身错了，不是数据 unlucky。

2.4 判决的执行——最见制度成色的部分

REJECTED 落地后发生了三件事，每件都值得讲：

  1. 假设族封禁：事件窗这一族假设进入"禁止复测"清单——不允许换个窗口定义、换个对照构造再申请一次 OOS。同一 OOS 窗口是消耗品，已经在这件事上花掉了。
  2. 数据资产保留：forecast + namechange 面板入库为可复用资产。否决的是假设，不是数据——数据没有立场，以后别的假设还能用。
  3. 衍生观察降级：过程中注意到"预告后反转"的苗头，但因未预注册、且属假设族内变体，标记为 hypothesis-generating（仅产生假设，不构成证据），禁止直接进入下一轮验证。想追，先写新预注册。

第 3 条最微妙，也最常被破坏："我在验证 A 的时候顺便看见 B 好像行"——这个"看见"本身已经消耗了数据的一次查看权。制度上的正确处理不是假装没看见，而是把它降级为假设、重新走全流程。顺便看见的东西不是证据，是线索。

3. 案例二：指数调样流 —— INCONCLUSIVE 3.1 假设

指数定期调样时，被动资金按公告名单集中买卖，造成可预测的短期价格压力（调样公告日到生效日之间的流入/流出流）。这是文献中有先例的现象（index rebalancing effect），先验等级比 AI 生成的叠加因子高一档（第三讲的结论二在此适用）。

3.2 流程与装配验证

这个案例多了一个真实工程环节：装配检验。调样流策略的输入是"公告名单 → 被动规模估算 → 流向符号"的拼装管线，任何一环错位（日期、方向、权重）都会无声地产出垃圾。装配管线先做了 PASS 检验（拼装结果与公告原文抽样比对），然后才进预注册。先验证数据管道，再验证策略假设——顺序不可反。

3.3 判决

发现期 +0.95%；OOS +1.00%，p = 0.062。INCONCLUSIVE——功效不足，冻结。

3.4 INCONCLUSIVE 的正确处理（比 REJECTED 难）

REJECTED 痛快，INCONCLUSIVE 折磨人——差 0.038 的 p 值，人性 screaming"再试一次"。制度规定：

  • 冻结，不许换口径重测：把窗口延长一年、换个统计检验、剔除某个月——每一个都是"看完结果再调规则"，正是第四讲锁死的研究者自由度
  • 不许宣布"基本有效"：对外口径只有三个词，INCONCLUSIVE 意味着不能写进任何汇报的"有效策略"栏
  • 唯一的两条出路：等新的前向数据积累（时间换功效），或写新预注册走前向轮（在下一轮真实调样发生前登记好门槛，用尚未发生的数据判定）

案例的实际处置：OOS 冻结，后续按前向路线重新预注册（2026-12 的调样轮在前向监控覆盖范围内）。"等"也是判决的一部分——接受"这个问题现在无法回答"，是多检验纪律里最反人性也最省钱的一条。

4. 三种判决的决策树（本章收束）

把第四讲到本讲的全部案例叠成一张裁决速查：

预注册验证结果
├─ 过全部门槛（DSR/副判据/分年/净费/正交）
│    → SUPPORTED → 影子监控 30 天（第四章）→ 部署决策
├─ 方向反 / 分年结构违规 / 正交后无残差
│    → REJECTED → 假设族封禁，数据保留，衍生观察降级
└─ 方向对但功效不足（p 略高、窗口短）
     → INCONCLUSIVE → 冻结：等前向数据 or 新预注册前向轮
                          （禁止：改门槛、改口径、原窗重测）

注意树里没有一条边通往"差不多就先小仓位上"。仓位不是验证的替代品——用真钱试探一个未判决的假设，等于用最大的成本做一次不可复现的实验。

5. 第二章总结
  • 独立验证 = 制度而非算力：预注册锁死自由度，DSR 校正选拔基数，OOS 一次性判定
  • 批量候选的结局（第五讲）：四层审计栈全灭，AI 工厂的合格产出是候选假设流
  • 单假设的结局（本讲）：REJECTED 封族留数据、INCONCLUSIVE 冻结等前向——判决的价值在执行
  • 唯一活下来的案例年化只有 2.37%：真 alpha 又小又难看；假 alpha 又大又合理

第二章证明了"诚实的验证"是可制度化执行的。第三章转向它的地基：当数据本身有问题时，再严格的验证也会被静默污染——双重复权、基准伪影、日期戳错位，五个真实的数据暗雷。

items.summary_html:
When an AI agent spends money, sends an email, or changes a record, someone eventually asks the same question: what exactly did it do, and can I trust this log? A normal log line can be edited after the fact. A receipt that is chained to the one before it cannot be edited quietly.

The idea

Each action gets a receipt. The receipt holds what was decided, the inputs the agent saw, who approved it, and a timestamp. It also holds the hash of the previous receipt. Change any old receipt and every hash after it stops matching.

import hashlib, json, time

def seal(prev_hash: str, action: dict) -> dict:
    body = {"ts": time.time(), "prev": prev_hash, "action": action}
    digest = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
    return {**body, "hash": digest}

def verify(chain: list[dict]) -> bool:
    prev = "genesis"
    for r in chain:
        body = {k: r[k] for k in ("ts", "prev", "action")}
        ok = r["prev"] == prev and r["hash"] == hashlib.sha256(
            json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
        if not ok:
            return False
        prev = r["hash"]
    return True
What to put in a receipt
  • The decision and the options that were considered, not only the winner.
  • The data the agent used (prices, documents, policy version) or a hash of it.
  • The human or policy that approved it.
  • The agent identity and the version of its instructions.
What it does not do

A hash chain shows that records were not changed after sealing. It does not prove the agent made a good decision, and it does not stop someone rewriting the whole chain from the start unless you anchor the latest hash somewhere you do not control (a timestamping service, a signed commit, a counterparty's copy). Keep that limit in mind when you describe it.

Where this shows up

Compliance rules for automated systems increasingly ask for logs of what a system did and why. Receipts like this are one way to keep those records in a form a third party can check without trusting you.

I write about agent audit trails and receipts for SYEN Systems (syensystems.com).

items.title: RD-AGENT 第五讲 · 三候选 DSR 全 FAIL 复盘：超额从哪来，又到哪去了
items.summary: 第五讲 · 三候选 DSR 全 FAIL 复盘：超额从哪来，又到哪去了 第二章 · 诚实的验证（第二讲） 学习目标：通过 A 股战役的完整复盘，看懂"排行榜很好看 → 独立验证全灭"的具体机制。 前置：第四讲。 1. 案例背景 A 股战役（2026-09-18~22）结束后，从 290 个因子的排行榜里，按预注册流程选出三个头部候选，送入独立验证管线。判定结果： 三候选 DSR 全部 FAIL。 这一讲的任务是把"全 FAIL"三个字拆开：每个候选的超额看起来从哪来、实际从哪来、验证时死在哪一刀下。 2. 第一刀：DSR——你试了多少次，就要还多少债 回顾第四讲：DSR 对 Sharpe 按试验次数 N 做校正。三个候选来自 290 个因子的排行榜头部，N 不是 3，是 290 （严格说还要算上每个因子的多次评估——第二讲看过， momentum_20d 一个因子就有 23 次评估，全池评估总次数以千计）。 直觉计算：即便候选的原始 Sharpe 在"单次检验"意义下显著，经过千次级别的试验基数校正后，所需门槛被推高到常规数字几乎不可能达到的水平。 这不是门槛苛刻，是事实如此 ——你在千次抛硬币里挑出的最好结果，本来就不该按单次抛硬币的标准评价。 三个候选全部倒在这一关。注意这一刀的 kill 逻辑 ：它不是说"这三个因子必然无效"，而是说" 从千次选拔里胜出的这三个，其成绩不足以证明自己不是运气 "。证据不足，按无罪推定的反面处理：不予采信。 3. 第二刀：归因分解——超额是 alpha 还是风格 beta 验证管线对候选做的第二件事：正交化检验（对已知风格因子回归，看残差）。战役中的组合级归因结果更极端： 等权合成组合 OOS IC 0.043，看似有效；但对 行业 + 低波 + 流动性 三个已知风格做正交后， 92% 的收益被解释掉 ，残差 alpha 的 t 值 = 0.14 。 翻译成人话：这个"AI 因子组合"赚的钱，九成二可以由"买了一堆低波动、高流动性股票、行业分布偏斜"复现——这三样都是几十年前就知道的东西，不需要 AI 一晚上算几百个因子。真正的残差部分，t=0.14，统计上就是零。 这是排行榜最惯用的魔术： 把风格 beta 包装成 alpha 卖给你 。排行榜不管你赚的是不是新钱——超额收益一列不区分"发现了别人不知道的东西"和"重仓了一个已知风格"。而后者你直接买低波 ETF 就有，不需要付因子挖掘的成本。 4. 第三刀：换手与成本——毛收益买不回净收益 第三讲埋过线：33 个版本的动量类因子是换手重灾区。验证管线在净费口径下复算：头部候选的换手率水平（战役实测约 40%+ 双边/调仓期）叠加 A 股交易成本后，毛超额被侵蚀到净口径不再显著。 排行榜展示的是毛收益或半净口径（第二讲的"三个必问"之二）。工厂没有动机展示净数字——它不知道你的费率，更因为净数字会让排行榜难看。 5. 最深的一刀：基准伪影（预告第八讲） 三候选验证期间还发现了一个更基础的问题： 基准本身有口径缺陷 （沪深 300 口径下剔除了涨停股），导致"超额"中有一块是基准定义制造的伪影。换成诚实口径重算后，双周 top200 组合 没有任何超额 。 第五讲 · 三候选 DSR 全 FAIL 复盘：超额从哪来，又到哪去了

第二章 · 诚实的验证（第二讲）
学习目标：通过 A 股战役的完整复盘，看懂"排行榜很好看 → 独立验证全灭"的具体机制。
前置：第四讲。

1. 案例背景

A 股战役（2026-09-18~22）结束后，从 290 个因子的排行榜里，按预注册流程选出三个头部候选，送入独立验证管线。判定结果：

三候选 DSR 全部 FAIL。

这一讲的任务是把"全 FAIL"三个字拆开：每个候选的超额看起来从哪来、实际从哪来、验证时死在哪一刀下。

2. 第一刀：DSR——你试了多少次，就要还多少债

回顾第四讲：DSR 对 Sharpe 按试验次数 N 做校正。三个候选来自 290 个因子的排行榜头部，N 不是 3，是 290（严格说还要算上每个因子的多次评估——第二讲看过，momentum_20d 一个因子就有 23 次评估，全池评估总次数以千计）。

直觉计算：即便候选的原始 Sharpe 在"单次检验"意义下显著，经过千次级别的试验基数校正后，所需门槛被推高到常规数字几乎不可能达到的水平。这不是门槛苛刻，是事实如此——你在千次抛硬币里挑出的最好结果，本来就不该按单次抛硬币的标准评价。

三个候选全部倒在这一关。注意这一刀的kill 逻辑：它不是说"这三个因子必然无效"，而是说"从千次选拔里胜出的这三个，其成绩不足以证明自己不是运气"。证据不足，按无罪推定的反面处理：不予采信。

3. 第二刀：归因分解——超额是 alpha 还是风格 beta

验证管线对候选做的第二件事：正交化检验（对已知风格因子回归，看残差）。战役中的组合级归因结果更极端：

等权合成组合 OOS IC 0.043，看似有效；但对行业 + 低波 + 流动性三个已知风格做正交后，92% 的收益被解释掉，残差 alpha 的 t 值 = 0.14。

翻译成人话：这个"AI 因子组合"赚的钱，九成二可以由"买了一堆低波动、高流动性股票、行业分布偏斜"复现——这三样都是几十年前就知道的东西，不需要 AI 一晚上算几百个因子。真正的残差部分，t=0.14，统计上就是零。

这是排行榜最惯用的魔术：把风格 beta 包装成 alpha 卖给你。排行榜不管你赚的是不是新钱——超额收益一列不区分"发现了别人不知道的东西"和"重仓了一个已知风格"。而后者你直接买低波 ETF 就有，不需要付因子挖掘的成本。

4. 第三刀：换手与成本——毛收益买不回净收益

第三讲埋过线：33 个版本的动量类因子是换手重灾区。验证管线在净费口径下复算：头部候选的换手率水平（战役实测约 40%+ 双边/调仓期）叠加 A 股交易成本后，毛超额被侵蚀到净口径不再显著。

排行榜展示的是毛收益或半净口径（第二讲的"三个必问"之二）。工厂没有动机展示净数字——它不知道你的费率，更因为净数字会让排行榜难看。

5. 最深的一刀：基准伪影（预告第八讲）

三候选验证期间还发现了一个更基础的问题：基准本身有口径缺陷（沪深 300 口径下剔除了涨停股），导致"超额"中有一块是基准定义制造的伪影。换成诚实口径重算后，双周 top200 组合没有任何超额。

这个发现的震撼在于它的层级：它不在"因子好不好"这一层，而在"超额这个量本身可不可信"这一层。因子验证做得再严格，基准错了，全部结论的地基就错了。完整展开留给第八讲——这里只需要记住教训的形状：验证要向下问到数据的地基，而不是停在因子这一层。

6. 复盘：四刀的层级结构

把四刀叠起来看，它们其实是一个自下而上的审计栈：

第 4 层  统计充分性   DSR / 多重检验校正     —— 成绩配得上选拔基数吗
第 3 层  收益来源     正交化 / 归因分解      —— 是新钱还是旧 beta
第 2 层  可实现性     换手 × 成本敏感性      —— 净费后还在吗
第 1 层  数据地基     基准口径 / 面板构建    —— 量本身可不可信

工厂的排行榜只在第 4 层之下活动，而且只做了一半（没有校正）。独立验证的价值就是把这个栈走完——三候选在四层上各挨了一刀，没有一个是"因子逻辑本身被证伪"，全部是证据与口径不合格。这正是第四讲那句话的实例：验证判的是"是不是真的"，不是"有多好"。

7. 军心稳定问题：全 FAIL 之后怎么办

全灭之后自然的情绪反应有两种，都要抵制：

  • "验证太苛刻，放宽门槛"——门槛放松 = 重新引入多重检验，全 FAIL 的结论本来就是"证据不足"，放宽标准不会让证据变足，只会让假阳性进门。
  • "AI 挖因子没用，弃了"——过度结论。正确读法：AI 工厂的价值主张需要重述。它的合格产出不是"可直接上线的因子"，而是"低成本生成的候选假设流"。从候选流到可部署策略之间，隔着一整条验证管线——这条管线以前也存在（人类研究员的 peer review + 实盘小仓试错），只是没人把它当成生产环节的一部分来正式建设。

战役的实际决策是第三条路：保留工厂、正式建设验证制度、把"诚实口径下零超额"如实记档——然后转向。转向后的第一个预注册实验（第六讲）和唯一存活的策略（第四章），都诞生在这套制度建立之后。

8. 本讲小结
  • 三候选死因四层级：DSR（千次选拔基数）、风格 beta 冒充 alpha（92% 被解释，残差 t=0.14）、净费侵蚀、基准伪影
  • 排行榜的魔术：不区分新钱与旧 beta、展示毛收益、不做选拔校正
  • 全 FAIL 的正确解读：AI 工厂的产出单位是"候选假设流"，不是"可上线因子"
  • 审计栈四层：统计充分性 → 收益来源 → 可实现性 → 数据地基，缺一层都可能漏杀

思考题：假如某候选通过了 DSR 和正交化，但净费后超额恰好为零（毛超额 = 成本）。你会判 SUPPORTED、REJECTED 还是 INCONCLUSIVE？给出理由。（没有标准答案——真实战役的裁决是按预注册里的门槛表逐项对照，想清楚"你的门槛表里有没有这一格"才是本题考点。）

items.summary: 第四讲 · 为什么需要独立验证：预注册与验证管线 第二章 · 诚实的验证（第一讲） 学习目标：理解"工厂自报成绩"与"独立验证"的制度差异；掌握预注册、DSR、样本外一次性判定等核心概念。 前置：第一章（尤其第二讲的"三个必问"）。 1. 从一个问题开始 第一章末尾留了一个数字：290 个因子，自报超额最高 +26.5%，独立验证零存活。这一讲回答： "独立验证"到底独立在哪，凭什么它的结论比工厂的数字更可信？ 先看一个对照。工厂回测和独立验证做的是相似的事——都是拿历史数据算因子收益。差别不在算力、不在代码质量，在 制度 ： 维度 工厂内置回测 独立验证管线 数据 战役面板（同一份） 独立拉取、独立清洗的复算面板 规则 可以边看结果边调（循环天然如此） 预注册 ：判定规则先写死、先存档 判定 排行榜排个序，没有门槛 一次性判定 ：门槛预注册，触发即终审 对象 每个因子都出数字 只验证通过初筛的极少数候选 结论性质 描述性的（"它收益多少"） 判决性的（"拒绝/不可判定/支持"） 一句话：工厂回测回答" 如果用它会怎样 "，独立验证回答" 它是不是真的 "。前者是描述，后者是统计判决。 2. 多重检验：为什么"边看边调"必然产出假阳性 这是全部验证科学的第一性原理，值得慢慢讲透。 设 290 个因子全部是纯噪声（与未来收益零相关）。每个因子在 5% 显著性水平下做检验，期望产出 290 × 0.05 ≈ 14.5 个"显著有效" 。这 14.5 个因子在排行榜上与真因子 长得一模一样 ——显著性不会在你脸上写"我是运气"。 人手动做研究时这个问题就存在（学术界管它叫 p-hacking 的温床）；LLM 循环把基数放大了两个数量级，把成本降到了零——于是多重检验从"需要警惕的偏差"升级成"系统的主导性失效模式"。 对付它的唯一制度化手段是预注册（pre-registration） ： 在看数据之前 ，把以下内容写成文档并存档：候选因子清单、验证用的数据窗口、判定门槛、统计口径、以及"如果不可判定怎么办" 验证时严格按存档执行， 禁止事后调整任何规则 规则改动 = 实验 identity 改变 = 必须整个重跑，旧结论作废 预注册的本质不是仪式感，是把 研究者的自由度（researcher degrees of freedom）在结果出来之前锁死 。你在第二讲见过的"参数可调的叠加因子"是在因子内部消耗自由度；"看完结果再决定用什么基准、什么窗口、什么门槛"是在验证环节消耗自由度——后者更隐蔽，杀伤力更大。 3. 验证管线的四个构件 以本课程配套的真实管线为例（AIResearchPlatform，与工厂分仓、独立拉数）： 构件一：独立数据复算 验证面板不从战役面板拷贝，而是从数据源独立拉取重算。原因直接来自实战：carry 因子 +18% 的双重复权 bug 藏在战役面板的构建代码里——如果验证直接消费这份面板，bug 会被原样继承，纠错永远不会发生。（口径问题的专题在第三章。） 构件二：预注册门槛 真实战役用到的门槛示例（写入预注册文档后才允许接触 OOS 数据）： DSR（Deflated Sharpe Ratio） ：对 Sharpe 做多重检验校正——你试了 N 个策略，显著性门槛就要相应抬高。N 越大，门槛越高，头名越难过线 主副裁判 ：主判据之外设一个口径不同的副判据（如价格口径 vs 资金费率口径），两者不一致时不得判"支持" 分年度约束 ：不允许"全部收益来自某一年"的结构——单年贡献超过上限即否决，防止把一段行情当成了规律 正交化对手 ：候选必须对已知风格因子（动量、价值、低波、流动性）做正交后仍有残差 alpha；被已有因子解释掉的部分不算新发现 构件三：样本外一次性判定（OOS 一次性） 样本外数据是 消耗品 ：每用一次就被污染一次。规范是一段 OOS 窗口只允许做一次判定—— 判 SUPPORTED：进入下一阶段（影子监控，第四章） 判 REJECTED：结论存档，该假设族进入"禁止复测"清单（防止换个马甲再试一次 OOS） 判 INCONCLUSIVE（如功效不足）：冻结，只能等新的前向数据或新预注册， 不允许降低门槛重试 构件四：留痕与可复现 验证报告落盘存档（数据指纹、代码版本、门槛数值），任何人任何时刻可复算。这不仅是科学规范，也是给自己未来的保险——第九讲会讲到，多个重大勘误（包括 +18% 假 carry）正是因为"历史结论可以复算"才被发现和纠正的。 4. 一次性判定的三份真实判决书 这套制度产出的三种结局，每种都有真实案例，构成接下来两讲的内容： 判决 案例 数字 讲次 REJECTED 业绩预告事件窗 OOS 价差 −0.49% （方向反），发现期亦无效 第六讲 INCONCLUSIVE 指数调样流 OOS +1.00% ，p=0.062——功效不足，冻结 第六讲 SUPPORTED crypto funding carry OOS +2.37%/年 ，p<0.0001，八项子检验全过 第四章 注意三个数字的相对量级： 唯一活下来的策略，年化 2.37% ；而被否决的两个，发现期的数字都远比它耀眼。真 alpha 又小又难看，假 alpha 又大又合理——这不是巧合，是这个行业的结构特征，后面每一讲都会回到这一点。 5. 本讲小结 工厂回测是描述，独立验证是判决；差别在制度不在算力 多重检验是循环挖掘的主导性失效模式，预注册是唯一的制度化解药 管线四构件：独立数据、预注册门槛（DSR/主副裁判/分年度/正交化对手）、OOS 一次性判定、留痕可复现 三种判决各有真实案例：REJECTED（−0.49%）、INCONCLUSIVE（+1.00%, p=0.062）、SUPPORTED（+2.37%/年） 思考题 ：你的同事说"DSR 门槛太严了，我们 290 个因子里一个都过不了，不如放宽到 10% 显著性水平"。请指出这段话里两处逻辑错误。（提示：门槛的功能是控制什么？改门槛等于做了什么？）

1. 从一个问题开始

第一章末尾留了一个数字：290 个因子，自报超额最高 +26.5%，独立验证零存活。这一讲回答："独立验证"到底独立在哪，凭什么它的结论比工厂的数字更可信？

先看一个对照。工厂回测和独立验证做的是相似的事——都是拿历史数据算因子收益。差别不在算力、不在代码质量，在制度：

维度 工厂内置回测 独立验证管线 数据 战役面板（同一份） 独立拉取、独立清洗的复算面板 规则 可以边看结果边调（循环天然如此） 预注册：判定规则先写死、先存档 判定 排行榜排个序，没有门槛 一次性判定：门槛预注册，触发即终审 对象 每个因子都出数字 只验证通过初筛的极少数候选 结论性质 描述性的（"它收益多少"） 判决性的（"拒绝/不可判定/支持"）

一句话：工厂回测回答"如果用它会怎样"，独立验证回答"它是不是真的"。前者是描述，后者是统计判决。

2. 多重检验：为什么"边看边调"必然产出假阳性

这是全部验证科学的第一性原理，值得慢慢讲透。

设 290 个因子全部是纯噪声（与未来收益零相关）。每个因子在 5% 显著性水平下做检验，期望产出 290 × 0.05 ≈ 14.5 个"显著有效"。这 14.5 个因子在排行榜上与真因子长得一模一样——显著性不会在你脸上写"我是运气"。

人手动做研究时这个问题就存在（学术界管它叫 p-hacking 的温床）；LLM 循环把基数放大了两个数量级，把成本降到了零——于是多重检验从"需要警惕的偏差"升级成"系统的主导性失效模式"。

对付它的唯一制度化手段是预注册（pre-registration）：

  1. 在看数据之前，把以下内容写成文档并存档：候选因子清单、验证用的数据窗口、判定门槛、统计口径、以及"如果不可判定怎么办"
  2. 验证时严格按存档执行，禁止事后调整任何规则
  3. 规则改动 = 实验 identity 改变 = 必须整个重跑，旧结论作废

预注册的本质不是仪式感，是把研究者的自由度（researcher degrees of freedom）在结果出来之前锁死。你在第二讲见过的"参数可调的叠加因子"是在因子内部消耗自由度；"看完结果再决定用什么基准、什么窗口、什么门槛"是在验证环节消耗自由度——后者更隐蔽，杀伤力更大。

3. 验证管线的四个构件

以本课程配套的真实管线为例（AIResearchPlatform，与工厂分仓、独立拉数）：

构件一：独立数据复算

验证面板不从战役面板拷贝，而是从数据源独立拉取重算。原因直接来自实战：carry 因子 +18% 的双重复权 bug 藏在战役面板的构建代码里——如果验证直接消费这份面板，bug 会被原样继承，纠错永远不会发生。（口径问题的专题在第三章。）

构件二：预注册门槛

真实战役用到的门槛示例（写入预注册文档后才允许接触 OOS 数据）：

  • DSR（Deflated Sharpe Ratio）：对 Sharpe 做多重检验校正——你试了 N 个策略，显著性门槛就要相应抬高。N 越大，门槛越高，头名越难过线
  • 主副裁判：主判据之外设一个口径不同的副判据（如价格口径 vs 资金费率口径），两者不一致时不得判"支持"
  • 分年度约束：不允许"全部收益来自某一年"的结构——单年贡献超过上限即否决，防止把一段行情当成了规律
  • 正交化对手：候选必须对已知风格因子（动量、价值、低波、流动性）做正交后仍有残差 alpha；被已有因子解释掉的部分不算新发现
构件三：样本外一次性判定（OOS 一次性）

样本外数据是消耗品：每用一次就被污染一次。规范是一段 OOS 窗口只允许做一次判定——

  • 判 SUPPORTED：进入下一阶段（影子监控，第四章）
  • 判 REJECTED：结论存档，该假设族进入"禁止复测"清单（防止换个马甲再试一次 OOS）
  • 判 INCONCLUSIVE（如功效不足）：冻结，只能等新的前向数据或新预注册，不允许降低门槛重试
构件四：留痕与可复现

验证报告落盘存档（数据指纹、代码版本、门槛数值），任何人任何时刻可复算。这不仅是科学规范，也是给自己未来的保险——第九讲会讲到，多个重大勘误（包括 +18% 假 carry）正是因为"历史结论可以复算"才被发现和纠正的。

4. 一次性判定的三份真实判决书

这套制度产出的三种结局，每种都有真实案例，构成接下来两讲的内容：

判决 案例 数字 讲次 REJECTED 业绩预告事件窗 OOS 价差 −0.49%（方向反），发现期亦无效 第六讲 INCONCLUSIVE 指数调样流 OOS +1.00%，p=0.062——功效不足，冻结 第六讲 SUPPORTED crypto funding carry OOS +2.37%/年，p<0.0001，八项子检验全过 第四章

注意三个数字的相对量级：唯一活下来的策略，年化 2.37%；而被否决的两个，发现期的数字都远比它耀眼。真 alpha 又小又难看，假 alpha 又大又合理——这不是巧合，是这个行业的结构特征，后面每一讲都会回到这一点。

5. 本讲小结
  • 工厂回测是描述，独立验证是判决；差别在制度不在算力
  • 多重检验是循环挖掘的主导性失效模式，预注册是唯一的制度化解药
  • 管线四构件：独立数据、预注册门槛（DSR/主副裁判/分年度/正交化对手）、OOS 一次性判定、留痕可复现
  • 三种判决各有真实案例：REJECTED（−0.49%）、INCONCLUSIVE（+1.00%, p=0.062）、SUPPORTED（+2.37%/年）

思考题：你的同事说"DSR 门槛太严了，我们 290 个因子里一个都过不了，不如放宽到 10% 显著性水平"。请指出这段话里两处逻辑错误。（提示：门槛的功能是控制什么？改门槛等于做了什么？）

items.title: Code Search RAG: Chunk by Function With tree-sitter, Not by 512 Tokens
items.summary:
Book: RAG Pocket Guide Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub The chunk the codebase assistant retrieved for "where does the retry delay get computed?" starts halfway down a function, at an except clause, and has no def line, no class name, nothing but a file path to say where it came from. The model writes a confident answer about a function it never saw the name of. The bug is in the chunker. It cut the file every 512 tokens, the way it cuts prose, and the cut landed in the middle of a function. Code has natural seams at def and class ; a token counter ignores them. The fix fits in two small files. Parse Python with tree-sitter , cut at function and class boundaries, carry the file path and the enclosing symbol as metadata, and split the definitions that are too big on statement boundaries. Then score both chunkers on a labelled query set, so you see the difference on your own machine instead of taking my word for it. What a token window does to a function A fixed window has no idea where a function starts. If a function begins at token 470 of a 512-token window, the chunk gets the decorator, the signature and four lines of body. The next chunk gets the rest of the body with no name attached. Ask for "the function that parses the config file" and the retriever has to match either a signature with no logic or logic with no signature. The cAST paper from Carnegie Mellon and Augment Code found the same problem: "Existing line-based chunking heuristics often break semantic structures, splitting functions or merging unrelated code." Their AST-based chunker, which splits large syntax nodes and merges small siblings under a size limit, reported a 4.3-point Recall@5 gain on RepoEval retrieval and a 2.67-point Pass@1 gain on SWE-bench generation over the fixed-size baseline. Frameworks have moved the same way. LlamaIndex ships a CodeSplitter that parses with tree-sitter and, in its source , caps chunks at 1,500 characters by default. The cAST authors published astchunk , which measures chunk size in non-whitespace characters and supports Python, Java, C# and TypeScript. Both are fine to use. Writing your own once is how you find out what they are doing for you, and how you tune it when your codebase has 600-line functions. Token windows cut wherever the count runs out. AST chunks cut where the code does. Two chunkers, same token budget Install the pieces. py-tree-sitter 0.26.0 needs Python 3.10 or newer, and the Python grammar ships as its own wheel. pip install tree-sitter tree-sitter-python \ sentence-transformers numpy The embedder is BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 : a small English model with 384 dimensions and a 512-token max sequence length. Both chunkers get the same budget of 480 tokens, counted with the embedder's own tokenizer, so a short header and the special tokens still fit under 512 and nothing gets silently truncated. That is the fair version of "512-token chunks". First file, chunkers.py , starting with the Chunk type: # chunkers.py from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import Callable import tree_sitter_python as tspython from tree_sitter import Language , Parser PARSER = Parser ( Language ( tspython . language ())) DEFS = { " function_definition " , " class_definition " } Count = Callable [[ str ], int ] @dataclass class Chunk : path : str symbol : str # "JSONDecoder.raw_decode", " ", or "" start : int # 1-based first line end : int # 1-based last line, inclusive text : str def embed_text ( self ) -> str : head = f " # { self . path } " if self . symbol : head += f " :: { self . symbol } " return f " { head } 
 { self . text } " The baseline comes next. It adds lines while their token count stays under the budget, emits a chunk, then backs up about 64 tokens for the overlap. The BGE tokenizer emits no token for a newline, so summing per line counts the same tokens the AST chunker counts on joined text: # chunkers.py (continued) def fixed_chunks ( path : str , src : str , ntok : Count , size : int = 480 , overlap : int = 64 ): lines = src . split ( " 
 " ) out , i = [], 0 while i < len ( lines ): j , used = i , 0 while j < len ( lines ): cost = ntok ( lines [ j ]) if used + cost > size and j > i : break used += cost j += 1 text = " 
 " . join ( lines [ i : j ]) out . append ( Chunk ( path , "" , i + 1 , j , text )) if j >= len ( lines ): break back , k = 0 , j while k > i + 1 and back < overlap : k -= 1 back += ntok ( lines [ k ]) i = k return out The baseline is slightly generous: it snaps to line ends and overlaps about 64 tokens, where a plain token splitter would cut mid-line. Its chunks still get the file path in the header. The only things it lacks are syntax-aware boundaries and the symbol name, which keeps the comparison about exactly those two things. src.split("
") rather than splitlines() is deliberate. tree-sitter counts rows by 
 only, and splitlines() also splits on form feeds, which some older Python files contain. Mixing the two puts every line number after the first form feed off by one. The AST chunker goes in the same file. First the helpers that write chunks: # chunkers.py (continued) def unwrap ( node ): if node . type == " decorated_definition " : return node . child_by_field_name ( " definition " ) return node def name_of ( defn ) -> str : return defn . child_by_field_name ( " name " ). text . decode () def ast_chunks ( path : str , src : str , ntok : Count , budget : int = 480 ): lines = src . split ( " 
 " ) tree = PARSER . parse ( src . encode ()) out : list [ Chunk ] = [] def span ( a , b ): # 0-based rows, inclusive return " 
 " . join ( lines [ a : b + 1 ]) def emit ( sym , a , b , head = "" ): body = span ( a , b ) if ntok ( head + body ) <= budget : out . append ( Chunk ( path , sym , a + 1 , b + 1 , head + body )) return # one statement is bigger than the budget: window it room = max ( budget - ntok ( head ), 64 ) for c in fixed_chunks ( path , body , ntok , size = room ): out . append ( Chunk ( path , sym , a + c . start , a + c . end , head + c . text )) emit writes one chunk when the span fits and falls back to line windows only when a single statement is bigger than the budget. pack sits on top of it and greedily groups neighbouring statements. It is still inside ast_chunks , so keep the indentation: # ast_chunks, continued def pack ( nodes , sym , head = "" ): group = [] for node in nodes : if group : a = group [ 0 ]. start_point [ 0 ] b = node . end_point [ 0 ] if ntok ( head + span ( a , b )) > budget : emit ( sym , a , group [ - 1 ]. end_point [ 0 ], head ) group = [] group . append ( node ) if group : emit ( sym , group [ 0 ]. start_point [ 0 ], group [ - 1 ]. end_point [ 0 ], head ) The last two helpers decide what a unit is, and the final line starts the walk at the module root: # ast_chunks, continued def define ( node , defn , scope ): name = name_of ( defn ) sym = f " { scope } . { name } " if scope else name a , b = node . start_point [ 0 ], node . end_point [ 0 ] if ntok ( span ( a , b )) <= budget : emit ( sym , a , b ) return body = defn . child_by_field_name ( " body " ) head = span ( a , body . start_point [ 0 ] - 1 ) + " 
 " if defn . type == " class_definition " : block ( body . named_children , sym , head ) else : pack ( body . named_children , sym , head ) def block ( nodes , scope , head = "" ): loose = [] for node in nodes : defn = unwrap ( node ) if defn . type in DEFS : if loose : pack ( loose , scope or " " , head ) loose = [] define ( node , defn , scope ) else : loose . append ( node ) if loose : pack ( loose , scope or " " , head ) block ( tree . root_node . named_children , "" ) return out Walk it top-down. block goes through the statements of a module or a class body. Each definition goes to define , and the statements between definitions (imports, constants, a class docstring) collect into loose and get packed into chunks or chunks named after the class. define emits a definition whole if it fits. Decorators count as part of the definition, because tree-sitter-python wraps them in a decorated_definition whose definition field holds the function or class. The symbol path is the breadcrumb. A method inside JSONDecoder gets JSONDecoder.raw_decode , and embed_text() puts # json/decoder.py :: JSONDecoder.raw_decode on the first line of what gets embedded. A query that says "JSON decoder" now has a literal match even when the method body never says it. When one function is bigger than the budget Function-level chunks break down on the big ones. A 300-line class or a 200-line function does not fit in 480 tokens, and dumping it whole into the embedder does not help. The model card for all-MiniLM-L6-v2 says so directly: "By default, input text longer than 256 word pieces is truncated." Everything past the cutoff is invisible to retrieval, and nothing warns you. The chunker above handles size in three steps. Too-big class: recurse. define calls block on the class body, so every method becomes its own chunk with a Class.method symbol. The class signature becomes a head that is prepended to the chunks of loose class-level statements, so the docstring and class attributes still say which class they belong to. Too-big function: pack statements under the signature. pack walks the body's top-level statements and greedily merges neighbours until the next one would blow the budget. Every piece starts with the full signature, decorators included. A retrieved piece from the middle of a long function still opens with def _make_iterencode(...) . This is the merge half of what cAST does: split big nodes, merge small siblings. Too-big single statement: fall back to windows. A 150-line if block is one statement. emit notices it does not fit and runs the line-window chunker over just that statement, with the signature still on top. cAST recurses into the statement's children instead, which keeps boundaries cleaner. The fallback is the cheap version; swap it for recursion when your codebase has a lot of these. Small siblings merge, big nodes split, and every split piece keeps the signature on top. Two costs to know about. The header eats budget, so a function with a 15-line signature leaves less room for the body in each piece. And pack re-tokenizes growing spans, which is quadratic in the worst case. On a few files that is nothing. On a monorepo, count tokens per statement once and add them up instead. Score both on a labelled query set A chunker is only better if retrieval gets better, so measure it. You need a corpus every reader already has, and the Python standard library is on your disk. The queries below describe what code does, mostly without using its identifiers, the way you search a codebase you did not write. Each label is a file plus a symbol path. Before the eval, append one helper to chunkers.py , so the gold line ranges come from the parser instead of from hand-typed line numbers: # chunkers.py (append) def symbols ( src : str ) -> dict [ str , tuple [ int , int ]]: found = {} def walk ( node , scope ): for child in node . named_children : defn = unwrap ( child ) if defn . type not in DEFS : continue name = name_of ( defn ) sym = f " { scope } . { name } " if scope else name found [ sym ] = ( child . start_point [ 0 ] + 1 , child . end_point [ 0 ] + 1 ) if defn . type == " class_definition " : walk ( defn . child_by_field_name ( " body " ), sym ) walk ( PARSER . parse ( src . encode ()). root_node , "" ) return found Second file, eval.py . The top holds the model, the files and the labels: # eval.py import sysconfig from pathlib import Path import numpy as np from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer from chunkers import ast_chunks , fixed_chunks , symbols MODEL = " BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 " QUERY = " Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: " FILES = [ " json/__init__.py " , " json/decoder.py " , " json/encoder.py " , " shlex.py " , " textwrap.py " , " collections/__init__.py " , ] LABELS = [ ( " quote a string so a POSIX shell sees one argument " , " shlex.py " , " quote " ), ( " split a command line into tokens like a shell " , " shlex.py " , " split " ), ( " strip the indentation shared by every line " , " textwrap.py " , " dedent " ), ( " break a paragraph into lines of a maximum width " , " textwrap.py " , " wrap " ), ( " add a prefix to the start of selected lines " , " textwrap.py " , " indent " ), ( " decode JSON at the start of a string, return end " , " json/decoder.py " , " JSONDecoder.raw_decode " ), ( " scan a JSON string literal handling escapes " , " json/decoder.py " , " py_scanstring " ), ( " serialize a Python object to a JSON str " , " json/__init__.py " , " dumps " ), ( " walk nested lists and dicts yielding JSON text " , " json/encoder.py " , " _make_iterencode " ), ( " the n elements with the highest counts " , " collections/__init__.py " , " Counter.most_common " ), ( " move a key to either end of an ordered dict " , " collections/__init__.py " , " OrderedDict.move_to_end " ), ( " make a tuple subclass with fields accessed by name " , " collections/__init__.py " , " namedtuple " ), ] recall embeds every chunk once, then checks the top five results for each query in two ways, explained after the code: # eval.py (continued) def recall ( chunks , gold , model , k = 5 ): vecs = model . encode ([ c . embed_text () for c in chunks ], normalize_embeddings = True ) touched = whole = 0 for query , path , ( s , e ) in gold : qv = model . encode ( QUERY + query , normalize_embeddings = True ) top = np . argsort ( - ( vecs @ qv ))[: k ] hits = [ chunks [ i ] for i in top if chunks [ i ]. path == path ] touched += any ( c . start <= e and c . end >= s for c in hits ) whole += any ( c . start <= s and c . end >= e for c in hits ) return touched / len ( gold ), whole / len ( gold ) main reads the six files from the standard library of whichever Python runs it and builds both chunk lists: # eval.py (continued) def main (): root = Path ( sysconfig . get_paths ()[ " stdlib " ]) model = SentenceTransformer ( MODEL ) def ntok ( text : str ) -> int : ids = model . tokenizer . encode ( text , add_special_tokens = False ) return len ( ids ) fixed , by_ast , spans = [], [], {} for rel in FILES : src = ( root / rel ). read_text ( encoding = " utf-8 " ) fixed += fixed_chunks ( rel , src , ntok ) by_ast += ast_chunks ( rel , src , ntok ) spans [ rel ] = symbols ( src ) gold = [( q , f , spans [ f ][ sym ]) for q , f , sym in LABELS ] for name , chunks in (( " fixed " , fixed ), ( " ast " , by_ast )): t , w = recall ( chunks , gold , model ) print ( f " { name : 5 } chunks= { len ( chunks ) : 4 } " f " touched@5= { t : . 2 f } whole@5= { w : . 2 f } " ) if __name__ == " __main__ " : main () The query prefix is the retrieval instruction from the BGE model card , which says passages need no prefix. Run python eval.py . The tokenizer may log a "sequence length is longer than" warning while counting tokens for whole classes; that is the counter measuring, not the embedder truncating. Read the two numbers separately. touched@5 asks whether any top-5 chunk overlaps the target function at all. That is lenient, and it is the metric a token-window chunker looks best on, because a chunk holding three lines of the right function counts. whole@5 asks whether one top-5 chunk contains the entire function, which is what the LLM needs in order to answer. The gap between them is the "body without its name" problem, measured. There are no results printed in this post, on purpose: your Python version changes the stdlib files, and 12 queries is a smoke test, not a benchmark. Run it and read your own numbers. Some labels are longer than the 480-token budget, so the AST chunker splits them too and neither chunker can score whole on them. namedtuple and _make_iterencode are the obvious ones; dumps (its docstring alone is long) and py_scanstring may be over as well, depending on your Python version. Expect that, and look at which chunk comes back instead. For a real decision, write 50 to 100 queries against your own repo, from real questions people asked in code review or on Slack, and keep the file in version control next to the chunker. Before you point it at your repo Four changes take this from a stdlib demo to something you would index a monorepo with. More languages. tree-sitter has grammars for most languages you will meet, but node type names differ per grammar. function_definition is the Python name; check each grammar's node-types.json and give every language its own DEFS set. If you want a maintained version for Python, Java, C# and TypeScript, astchunk already does it. Parse errors. tree-sitter is built to keep producing useful results even when the source has syntax errors , so a half-written file mid-refactor still produces a tree. py-tree-sitter exposes has_error on every node. Check it on the root, and when a file is badly broken, fall back to fixed_chunks for that file rather than indexing garbage boundaries. A code-aware embedder. bge-small-en-v1.5 is a general English model with a WordPiece tokenizer that shreds snake_case and camelCase into fragments. It works for the demo. For production, compare a code-trained embedding model on your labelled set using the same eval.py ; that is what the set is for. Keyword search next to vectors. Exact identifiers, error codes and config keys are where dense retrieval is weakest. Index the symbol field in a keyword index too and fuse the results. A query that contains raw_decode should find raw_decode without asking an embedding model to guess. If this was useful A retriever can only return what the chunker kept together, and code makes that easy to see. The RAG Pocket Guide covers the stages on either side of this one, retrieval and reranking, plus the chunking patterns for production RAG. If you are building search over a codebase or anything else with structure, it is the short version of the decisions this post only touches.

Their AST-based chunker, which splits large syntax nodes and merges small siblings under a size limit, reported a 4.3-point Recall@5 gain on RepoEval retrieval and a 2.67-point Pass@1 gain on SWE-bench generation over the fixed-size baseline.

Frameworks have moved the same way. LlamaIndex ships a CodeSplitter that parses with tree-sitter and, in its source, caps chunks at 1,500 characters by default. The cAST authors published astchunk, which measures chunk size in non-whitespace characters and supports Python, Java, C# and TypeScript. Both are fine to use. Writing your own once is how you find out what they are doing for you, and how you tune it when your codebase has 600-line functions.


Token windows cut wherever the count runs out. AST chunks cut where the code does.

Two chunkers, same token budget

Install the pieces. py-tree-sitter 0.26.0 needs Python 3.10 or newer, and the Python grammar ships as its own wheel.

pip install tree-sitter tree-sitter-python \
  sentence-transformers numpy

The embedder is BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5: a small English model with 384 dimensions and a 512-token max sequence length. Both chunkers get the same budget of 480 tokens, counted with the embedder's own tokenizer, so a short header and the special tokens still fit under 512 and nothing gets silently truncated. That is the fair version of "512-token chunks".

First file, chunkers.py, starting with the Chunk type:

# chunkers.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Callable

import tree_sitter_python as tspython
from tree_sitter import Language, Parser

PARSER = Parser(Language(tspython.language()))
DEFS = {"function_definition", "class_definition"}
Count = Callable[[str], int]

@dataclass
class Chunk:
    path: str
    symbol: str  # "JSONDecoder.raw_decode", "", or ""
    start: int   # 1-based first line
    end: int     # 1-based last line, inclusive
    text: str

    def embed_text(self) -> str:
        head = f"# {self.path}"
        if self.symbol:
            head += f" :: {self.symbol}"
        return f"{head}\n{self.text}"

The baseline comes next. It adds lines while their token count stays under the budget, emits a chunk, then backs up about 64 tokens for the overlap. The BGE tokenizer emits no token for a newline, so summing per line counts the same tokens the AST chunker counts on joined text:

# chunkers.py (continued)
def fixed_chunks(path: str, src: str, ntok: Count,
                 size: int = 480, overlap: int = 64):
    lines = src.split("\n")
    out, i = [], 0
    while i < len(lines):
        j, used = i, 0
        while j < len(lines):
            cost = ntok(lines[j])
            if used + cost > size and j > i:
                break
            used += cost
            j += 1
        text = "\n".join(lines[i:j])
        out.append(Chunk(path, "", i + 1, j, text))
        if j >= len(lines):
            break
        back, k = 0, j
        while k > i + 1 and back < overlap:
            k -= 1
            back += ntok(lines[k])
        i = k
    return out

The baseline is slightly generous: it snaps to line ends and overlaps about 64 tokens, where a plain token splitter would cut mid-line. Its chunks still get the file path in the header. The only things it lacks are syntax-aware boundaries and the symbol name, which keeps the comparison about exactly those two things.

src.split("\n") rather than splitlines() is deliberate. tree-sitter counts rows by \n only, and splitlines() also splits on form feeds, which some older Python files contain. Mixing the two puts every line number after the first form feed off by one.

The AST chunker goes in the same file. First the helpers that write chunks:

# chunkers.py (continued)
def unwrap(node):
    if node.type == "decorated_definition":
        return node.child_by_field_name("definition")
    return node

def name_of(defn) -> str:
    return defn.child_by_field_name("name").text.decode()

def ast_chunks(path: str, src: str, ntok: Count,
               budget: int = 480):
    lines = src.split("\n")
    tree = PARSER.parse(src.encode())
    out: list[Chunk] = []

    def span(a, b):  # 0-based rows, inclusive
        return "\n".join(lines[a:b + 1])

    def emit(sym, a, b, head=""):
        body = span(a, b)
        if ntok(head + body) <= budget:
            out.append(Chunk(path, sym, a + 1, b + 1, head + body))
            return
        # one statement is bigger than the budget: window it
        room = max(budget - ntok(head), 64)
        for c in fixed_chunks(path, body, ntok, size=room):
            out.append(Chunk(path, sym, a + c.start, a + c.end,
                             head + c.text))

emit writes one chunk when the span fits and falls back to line windows only when a single statement is bigger than the budget. pack sits on top of it and greedily groups neighbouring statements. It is still inside ast_chunks, so keep the indentation:

    # ast_chunks, continued
    def pack(nodes, sym, head=""):
        group = []
        for node in nodes:
            if group:
                a = group[0].start_point[0]
                b = node.end_point[0]
                if ntok(head + span(a, b)) > budget:
                    emit(sym, a, group[-1].end_point[0], head)
                    group = []
            group.append(node)
        if group:
            emit(sym, group[0].start_point[0],
                 group[-1].end_point[0], head)

The last two helpers decide what a unit is, and the final line starts the walk at the module root:

    # ast_chunks, continued
    def define(node, defn, scope):
        name = name_of(defn)
        sym = f"{scope}.{name}" if scope else name
        a, b = node.start_point[0], node.end_point[0]
        if ntok(span(a, b)) <= budget:
            emit(sym, a, b)
            return
        body = defn.child_by_field_name("body")
        head = span(a, body.start_point[0] - 1) + "\n"
        if defn.type == "class_definition":
            block(body.named_children, sym, head)
        else:
            pack(body.named_children, sym, head)

    def block(nodes, scope, head=""):
        loose = []
        for node in nodes:
            defn = unwrap(node)
            if defn.type in DEFS:
                if loose:
                    pack(loose, scope or "", head)
                    loose = []
                define(node, defn, scope)
            else:
                loose.append(node)
        if loose:
            pack(loose, scope or "", head)

    block(tree.root_node.named_children, "")
    return out

Walk it top-down. block goes through the statements of a module or a class body. Each definition goes to define, and the statements between definitions (imports, constants, a class docstring) collect into loose and get packed into chunks or chunks named after the class. define emits a definition whole if it fits. Decorators count as part of the definition, because tree-sitter-python wraps them in a decorated_definition whose definition field holds the function or class.

The symbol path is the breadcrumb. A method inside JSONDecoder gets JSONDecoder.raw_decode, and embed_text() puts # json/decoder.py :: JSONDecoder.raw_decode on the first line of what gets embedded. A query that says "JSON decoder" now has a literal match even when the method body never says it.

When one function is bigger than the budget

Function-level chunks break down on the big ones. A 300-line class or a 200-line function does not fit in 480 tokens, and dumping it whole into the embedder does not help. The model card for all-MiniLM-L6-v2 says so directly: "By default, input text longer than 256 word pieces is truncated." Everything past the cutoff is invisible to retrieval, and nothing warns you.

The chunker above handles size in three steps.

Too-big class: recurse. define calls block on the class body, so every method becomes its own chunk with a Class.method symbol. The class signature becomes a head that is prepended to the chunks of loose class-level statements, so the docstring and class attributes still say which class they belong to.

Too-big function: pack statements under the signature. pack walks the body's top-level statements and greedily merges neighbours until the next one would blow the budget. Every piece starts with the full signature, decorators included. A retrieved piece from the middle of a long function still opens with def _make_iterencode(...). This is the merge half of what cAST does: split big nodes, merge small siblings.

Too-big single statement: fall back to windows. A 150-line if block is one statement. emit notices it does not fit and runs the line-window chunker over just that statement, with the signature still on top. cAST recurses into the statement's children instead, which keeps boundaries cleaner. The fallback is the cheap version; swap it for recursion when your codebase has a lot of these.


Small siblings merge, big nodes split, and every split piece keeps the signature on top.

Two costs to know about. The header eats budget, so a function with a 15-line signature leaves less room for the body in each piece. And pack re-tokenizes growing spans, which is quadratic in the worst case. On a few files that is nothing. On a monorepo, count tokens per statement once and add them up instead.

Score both on a labelled query set

A chunker is only better if retrieval gets better, so measure it. You need a corpus every reader already has, and the Python standard library is on your disk. The queries below describe what code does, mostly without using its identifiers, the way you search a codebase you did not write. Each label is a file plus a symbol path.

Before the eval, append one helper to chunkers.py, so the gold line ranges come from the parser instead of from hand-typed line numbers:

# chunkers.py (append)
def symbols(src: str) -> dict[str, tuple[int, int]]:
    found = {}

    def walk(node, scope):
        for child in node.named_children:
            defn = unwrap(child)
            if defn.type not in DEFS:
                continue
            name = name_of(defn)
            sym = f"{scope}.{name}" if scope else name
            found[sym] = (child.start_point[0] + 1,
                          child.end_point[0] + 1)
            if defn.type == "class_definition":
                walk(defn.child_by_field_name("body"), sym)

    walk(PARSER.parse(src.encode()).root_node, "")
    return found

Second file, eval.py. The top holds the model, the files and the labels:

# eval.py
import sysconfig
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

from chunkers import ast_chunks, fixed_chunks, symbols

MODEL = "BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5"
QUERY = "Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: "
FILES = [
    "json/__init__.py", "json/decoder.py", "json/encoder.py",
    "shlex.py", "textwrap.py", "collections/__init__.py",
]
LABELS = [
    ("quote a string so a POSIX shell sees one argument",
     "shlex.py", "quote"),
    ("split a command line into tokens like a shell",
     "shlex.py", "split"),
    ("strip the indentation shared by every line",
     "textwrap.py", "dedent"),
    ("break a paragraph into lines of a maximum width",
     "textwrap.py", "wrap"),
    ("add a prefix to the start of selected lines",
     "textwrap.py", "indent"),
    ("decode JSON at the start of a string, return end",
     "json/decoder.py", "JSONDecoder.raw_decode"),
    ("scan a JSON string literal handling escapes",
     "json/decoder.py", "py_scanstring"),
    ("serialize a Python object to a JSON str",
     "json/__init__.py", "dumps"),
    ("walk nested lists and dicts yielding JSON text",
     "json/encoder.py", "_make_iterencode"),
    ("the n elements with the highest counts",
     "collections/__init__.py", "Counter.most_common"),
    ("move a key to either end of an ordered dict",
     "collections/__init__.py", "OrderedDict.move_to_end"),
    ("make a tuple subclass with fields accessed by name",
     "collections/__init__.py", "namedtuple"),
]

recall embeds every chunk once, then checks the top five results for each query in two ways, explained after the code:

# eval.py (continued)
def recall(chunks, gold, model, k=5):
    vecs = model.encode([c.embed_text() for c in chunks],
                        normalize_embeddings=True)
    touched = whole = 0
    for query, path, (s, e) in gold:
        qv = model.encode(QUERY + query, normalize_embeddings=True)
        top = np.argsort(-(vecs @ qv))[:k]
        hits = [chunks[i] for i in top if chunks[i].path == path]
        touched += any(c.start <= e and c.end >= s for c in hits)
        whole += any(c.start <= s and c.end >= e for c in hits)
    return touched / len(gold), whole / len(gold)

main reads the six files from the standard library of whichever Python runs it and builds both chunk lists:

# eval.py (continued)
def main():
    root = Path(sysconfig.get_paths()["stdlib"])
    model = SentenceTransformer(MODEL)

    def ntok(text: str) -> int:
        ids = model.tokenizer.encode(text, add_special_tokens=False)
        return len(ids)

    fixed, by_ast, spans = [], [], {}
    for rel in FILES:
        src = (root / rel).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        fixed += fixed_chunks(rel, src, ntok)
        by_ast += ast_chunks(rel, src, ntok)
        spans[rel] = symbols(src)

    gold = [(q, f, spans[f][sym]) for q, f, sym in LABELS]
    for name, chunks in (("fixed", fixed), ("ast", by_ast)):
        t, w = recall(chunks, gold, model)
        print(f"{name:5} chunks={len(chunks):4} "
              f"touched@5={t:.2f} whole@5={w:.2f}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The query prefix is the retrieval instruction from the BGE model card, which says passages need no prefix. Run python eval.py. The tokenizer may log a "sequence length is longer than" warning while counting tokens for whole classes; that is the counter measuring, not the embedder truncating.

Read the two numbers separately. touched@5 asks whether any top-5 chunk overlaps the target function at all. That is lenient, and it is the metric a token-window chunker looks best on, because a chunk holding three lines of the right function counts. whole@5 asks whether one top-5 chunk contains the entire function, which is what the LLM needs in order to answer. The gap between them is the "body without its name" problem, measured.

There are no results printed in this post, on purpose: your Python version changes the stdlib files, and 12 queries is a smoke test, not a benchmark. Run it and read your own numbers. Some labels are longer than the 480-token budget, so the AST chunker splits them too and neither chunker can score whole on them. namedtuple and _make_iterencode are the obvious ones; dumps (its docstring alone is long) and py_scanstring may be over as well, depending on your Python version. Expect that, and look at which chunk comes back instead. For a real decision, write 50 to 100 queries against your own repo, from real questions people asked in code review or on Slack, and keep the file in version control next to the chunker.

Before you point it at your repo

Four changes take this from a stdlib demo to something you would index a monorepo with.

More languages. tree-sitter has grammars for most languages you will meet, but node type names differ per grammar. function_definition is the Python name; check each grammar's node-types.json and give every language its own DEFS set. If you want a maintained version for Python, Java, C# and TypeScript, astchunk already does it.

Parse errors. tree-sitter is built to keep producing useful results even when the source has syntax errors, so a half-written file mid-refactor still produces a tree. py-tree-sitter exposes has_error on every node. Check it on the root, and when a file is badly broken, fall back to fixed_chunks for that file rather than indexing garbage boundaries.

A code-aware embedder. bge-small-en-v1.5 is a general English model with a WordPiece tokenizer that shreds snake_case and camelCase into fragments. It works for the demo. For production, compare a code-trained embedding model on your labelled set using the same eval.py; that is what the set is for.

Keyword search next to vectors. Exact identifiers, error codes and config keys are where dense retrieval is weakest. Index the symbol field in a keyword index too and fuse the results. A query that contains raw_decode should find raw_decode without asking an embedding model to guess.

If this was useful

A retriever can only return what the chunker kept together, and code makes that easy to see. The RAG Pocket Guide covers the stages on either side of this one, retrieval and reranking, plus the chunking patterns for production RAG. If you are building search over a codebase or anything else with structure, it is the short version of the decisions this post only touches.

items.title: Building TrialBridge: An AI clinical trial matcher built in a single hack day
items.summary: We, Team Latent, built TrialBridge during the Hacktoberfest Hack Day Coimbatore x (INIT Club & IDEA Club). We wanted to tackle a problem that actually matters: cancer treatments often push Indian families into debt, while slots for free, cutting-edge clinical trials go unfilled. The barrier is the data—eligibility rules are dense pages of medical jargon that patients can't understand and busy oncologists rarely have time to read. Here is how our team built an AI-powered screening aid to bridge that gap. How it works: Our stack is Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, and zod. Intake: Users upload photos of their medical reports, scans, and current prescriptions. To stay within Vercel's hosting request-size limits, we shrink the photos directly in the browser before they hit the backend. Registry Data: We pull active, recruiting trials with open (or opening soon) Indian sites directly from the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API. The Logic: We built a custom text splitter (lib/criteria.ts) to break down the massive blocks of registry text into atomic inclusion and exclusion rules. The Output: The app generates a printable summary for the oncologist, complete with a ✓ / ✗ / ? checklist for every rule. It even checks trial rules against the patient's current medicines (accounting for end dates and washout periods) to generate specific questions for the doctor. Safety First: The app never claims true medical eligibility—it only says "may qualify, confirm with your oncologist". The Gemma 4 Partner Challenge We submitted this for the Best Use of Gemma challenge. We used Google's open-weight gemma-4-26b-a4b-it model via the Gemini API to do the heavy lifting. First, Gemma performs multimodal extraction, reading the uploaded images to build a structured patient profile (cancer type, stage, biomarkers, ECOG, labs, current medicines) alongside the exact quotes it used as evidence. The user manually checks this profile before any matching happens. Then, Gemma judges the patient against each eligibility rule separately. A crucial architectural decision we made was keeping the AI strictly as a rule-judge, while plain, unit-tested code decides the final trial outcome (likely match, possible match, or not eligible). Stuff that broke (and how we fixed it) Building this in a day meant hitting a lot of walls. Here is what we learned: Latency: Our first parallel runs took about 3 minutes per trial. We fixed this by switching Gemma to minimal thinking mode and writing medical hints directly into the prompt (e.g., "stage IV means metastatic"). This dropped a 4-trial batch down to 42 seconds with no thinking tokens used. Double Negatives: Asking the AI "does the patient pass this exclusion rule?" was ambiguous and caused errors. We changed the prompt to simply ask "does this exclusion apply?" and flipped the boolean in our code. Free-Tier Rate Limits: On our first live run, Gemma's free tier got busy and threw 429 errors. We handled this by building automatic retries with a UI countdown. We also added a "quick first look" prompt to filter out obvious mismatches early, which narrowed 20 trials down to 4 full checks. Drug Washout Windows: The model initially treated completed drug courses as current. Injecting today's exact date into the prompt fixed it, allowing Gemma to correctly calculate washout periods. Messy Registry Text: Real registry criteria are full of escaped characters, mixed headings, and nested sub-rules. We had to refine our text splitter against a sanity run of 33 trials and 579 rules to finally get clean data. Links Live Demo: https://trialbridge-beta.vercel.app GitHub Repo: https://github.com/vipinsudhakar/hacktoberfest-hack-day-coimbatore-x-init-club-and-idea-club Demo Video: https://youtu.be/EAS2rQpnZYA Huge thanks to the team for surviving the sprint! @vipinsudhakar007 @shashank69420 @akshara_sree_30 (Built for Hacktoberfest Hack Day Coimbatore x (INIT Club & IDEA Club) 2026)

We, Team Latent, built TrialBridge during the Hacktoberfest Hack Day Coimbatore x (INIT Club & IDEA Club). We wanted to tackle a problem that actually matters: cancer treatments often push Indian families into debt, while slots for free, cutting-edge clinical trials go unfilled. The barrier is the data—eligibility rules are dense pages of medical jargon that patients can't understand and busy oncologists rarely have time to read.

Here is how our team built an AI-powered screening aid to bridge that gap.

How it works:

Our stack is Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, and zod.

Intake: Users upload photos of their medical reports, scans, and current prescriptions. To stay within Vercel's hosting request-size limits, we shrink the photos directly in the browser before they hit the backend.

Registry Data: We pull active, recruiting trials with open (or opening soon) Indian sites directly from the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API.

The Logic: We built a custom text splitter (lib/criteria.ts) to break down the massive blocks of registry text into atomic inclusion and exclusion rules.

The Output: The app generates a printable summary for the oncologist, complete with a ✓ / ✗ / ? checklist for every rule. It even checks trial rules against the patient's current medicines (accounting for end dates and washout periods) to generate specific questions for the doctor.

Safety First: The app never claims true medical eligibility—it only says "may qualify, confirm with your oncologist".

The Gemma 4 Partner Challenge
We submitted this for the Best Use of Gemma challenge. We used Google's open-weight gemma-4-26b-a4b-it model via the Gemini API to do the heavy lifting.

First, Gemma performs multimodal extraction, reading the uploaded images to build a structured patient profile (cancer type, stage, biomarkers, ECOG, labs, current medicines) alongside the exact quotes it used as evidence. The user manually checks this profile before any matching happens.

Then, Gemma judges the patient against each eligibility rule separately. A crucial architectural decision we made was keeping the AI strictly as a rule-judge, while plain, unit-tested code decides the final trial outcome (likely match, possible match, or not eligible).

Stuff that broke (and how we fixed it)
Building this in a day meant hitting a lot of walls. Here is what we learned:

Latency: Our first parallel runs took about 3 minutes per trial. We fixed this by switching Gemma to minimal thinking mode and writing medical hints directly into the prompt (e.g., "stage IV means metastatic"). This dropped a 4-trial batch down to 42 seconds with no thinking tokens used.

Double Negatives: Asking the AI "does the patient pass this exclusion rule?" was ambiguous and caused errors. We changed the prompt to simply ask "does this exclusion apply?" and flipped the boolean in our code.

Free-Tier Rate Limits: On our first live run, Gemma's free tier got busy and threw 429 errors. We handled this by building automatic retries with a UI countdown. We also added a "quick first look" prompt to filter out obvious mismatches early, which narrowed 20 trials down to 4 full checks.

Drug Washout Windows: The model initially treated completed drug courses as current. Injecting today's exact date into the prompt fixed it, allowing Gemma to correctly calculate washout periods.

Messy Registry Text: Real registry criteria are full of escaped characters, mixed headings, and nested sub-rules. We had to refine our text splitter against a sanity run of 33 trials and 579 rules to finally get clean data.
