items.title: LLM Regression Testing for Jira with CogniRunner
items.summary: LLM regression testing means running the same labelled inputs again after you change a prompt or a model, to see what the change broke. This tutorial does that for an AI check on a Jira workflow validator. Here the test set is a Jira filter of 8 labelled requests. An 80-line Node script runs it. Each call goes to CogniRunner's rule test over REST, which reads the issue, asks the model and writes nothing to Jira. I ran it on 13 October 2026 because I wanted to move a validator from openai/gpt-6-luna to anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5. Over three rounds, the site's model matched 6, 7 and 7 of the 8 labels. The candidate matched 8 of 8. I built the test expecting the candidate to miss, and it was the site's model that missed (I'd have bet the other way). I found the cause in the rule, and I don't think it says much about either model. Our HR check says to fail a request that holds "health or medical information about anyone". Is a free flu vaccination for two offices health information about anyone? Our rule didn't say. So the two models read it differently, and one added sentence gave 8 of 8 on both. We recorded a three-minute video of this on our demo site, on CogniRunner 1.34.0. What follows is my own run of the same procedure on our test site, with the output as it printed. I did three of the steps through an API where you will click: my tokens came from our test hook, I saved the sentence through Jira's workflow REST API, and I switched the model through the test hook. The video shows those screens, and I give the timestamp at each step. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lMpvV03upQA [!NOTE] Prerequisites A Jira Cloud site with CogniRunner 1.34.0 or later. The Marketplace calls that build 7.16.0, released 12 October 2026. I ran a development build of 1.34.0 on our test site. An AI provider saved in CogniRunner's Settings. Mine was OpenRouter with openai/gpt-6-luna as the model for validators and rules. If you haven't set one up, the provider tutorial covers it. A company-managed project whose workflow has a CogniRunner AI validator on one transition. Mine was called Send for Review. An email and API token for Jira's REST API. The script reads the published workflow. I ran it as a Jira admin. A CogniRunner admin, to create the REST API token in step 2. Node 18 or later. I used Node v24.15.0. The script has no dependencies. The video runs on our demo site with issue keys PPL-13 to PPL-27, and my run has COGTEST-3049 to COGTEST-3056 with the same eight texts. Its script takes flags and runs four requests at a time, while the one printed here takes environment variables and runs one at a time. In the video the first round is 7 of 8. Mine was 6 of 8. [[steps]] Build the golden dataset — eight requests in a Jira filter, each labelled expect-pass or expect-block. Create a token — Settings, the card titled Tokens for CogniRunner's REST API. Save the script — it reads the saved rule from Jira and calls the rule test for each request. Run the baseline — the site's own model, three rounds. Run the candidate — one variable, and the site's model stays as it is. Read the mismatch — decide whether the model or the rule is wrong. Try the sentence, save it, run both again — first unsaved, then saved. Switch the site's model — and find the switch and the tests in the audit log. What one rule test does: one field, one prompt, nothing written A CogniRunner AI validator sits on a workflow transition. Somebody moves the request. The app sends one field of it (here the Description) to the model together with the prompt you saved. Back comes pass or fail, with a reason. Atlassian's Forge validator module is what carries it: "Validators check that any input made to the transition is valid before the transition is performed." You may know the Test button in the rule editor. CogniRunner's Rules REST API has the same thing as a call: POST ?resource=rules&action=test . Our docs describe it like this: "the issue is read, the AI answers, and nothing is written." The body carries the issue key, the field and the prompt. Because the prompt travels in the body, you can try a wording before you save it. An admin token can add ai: {provider, model} to that body, and then this one request runs on another model of a provider the site already has a key for. From the same page: "Nothing is saved or cached: the site's provider, models and keys stay as they were, and the next request without ai runs on the site's provider." So the whole procedure is a loop over a filter. The same call takes other kinds of rule as well, and I tested validators. The rest of this API is in the release post for Marketplace version 3.3.0 and on the product page . Another thing you can do to the same validator is hand it a document, and the tutorial on giving one an API spec covers that. Step 1. Build the golden dataset: a Jira filter of 8 labelled issues People who test LLM apps call a fixed set of inputs with known right answers a golden dataset. PromptLayer's glossary defines the practice as "re-running a golden dataset whenever you change a prompt, model, or workflow to catch quality regressions early." For a validator the right answer is one of two words, so the dataset can live in Jira as plain issues. Create eight requests in the project the validator guards. Give each the label gate-test , and then expect-pass or expect-block . Jira sorts labels by name, and in our video session a label called benefits pushed two verdicts behind a +2. Is eight enough? Probably not for a rule that matters a lot. Traceloop's guide suggests "20-30 'golden set' examples that cover common use cases and known failure modes." Our eight came out of 28 candidates. Our video session ran those 28 on both models, 600 dry runs in all. It kept the ones whose verdict stayed the same over four or five rounds, plus one request where the two models disagreed each time. A vaccination is a health care service. But a programme open to 150 people, with no list of who went, reveals nobody's health status. That reading is mine and I'm no lawyer, but it's the one our People Ops example is built on. The rule left room for both readings, and I think each model took one. What this set doesn't test A validator reads one field. Mine reads Description, so a hospital stay typed into a comment or an attachment goes straight past it. Treat the check as a quality gate before HR approves. I wouldn't call it a security control. A dry run takes as long as the model takes. A live transition allows 20 seconds. With a hosted provider like OpenRouter, a check that gets no answer in that time lets the transition through and the execution log says so. Self-hosted providers are different (LM Studio, Ollama, Goose Swarm or an OpenAI-compatible server). For those, 1.34.0 added a hold you can turn on. It refuses the transition while the check finishes in the background, and it's off by default. My slowest dry run was 9.4 seconds, so neither case came up. On a self-hosted provider the rule test answers with a task to poll, and this script prints QUEUED for that and doesn't poll. I didn't make a real transition on this run. Our video session did, on 12 October, on the demo site. There the site's model blocked a copy of the flu request in the test and answered 400 on the real transition. With the candidate set, the test passed and the request moved for real. So I have one pair, a day old. Jira has nothing like this built in that I could find. Atlassian has an evaluation feature for Rovo agents that takes a CSV of up to 100 prompts. It's for agents. Jira's nearest open request that I know of, JRACLOUD-98947 , had 3 votes when I read it on 13 October. What you have now [[takeaways]] A Jira filter that is your validator's test set: eight requests, each labelled with the verdict you expect. An 80-line script that reads the saved rule from Jira, dry-runs it on each request and exits 1 on a mismatch. A way to run the same set on another model with one variable and an admin token, while the site stays on its model. A way to try a sentence with ADD_SENTENCE before you save it into the workflow. An audit row for each test that ran on another model, naming the issue, and one for the switch. A baseline you ran three times, so you know which misses are stable. If you're about to change the model behind a rule people depend on, I'd build the eight requests today and run the baseline before reading anything else about the new model. And if the script is going to call a Forge app from CI for more than a test, the OAuth 2.0 tutorial shows the other way in. Originally published on leanzero.net . More Atlassian, Forge and local-AI write-ups at leanzero.net/blog , and if you're planning a migration or a Forge app, that's what we do: leanzero.net/services .
items.summary_html:
LLM regression testing means running the same labelled inputs again after you change a prompt or a model, to see what the change broke. This tutorial does that for an AI check on a Jira workflow validator. Here the test set is a Jira filter of 8 labelled requests. An 80-line Node script runs it. Each call goes to CogniRunner's rule test over REST, which reads the issue, asks the model and writes nothing to Jira.

I ran it on 13 October 2026 because I wanted to move a validator from openai/gpt-6-luna to anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5. Over three rounds, the site's model matched 6, 7 and 7 of the 8 labels. The candidate matched 8 of 8. I built the test expecting the candidate to miss, and it was the site's model that missed (I'd have bet the other way).

I found the cause in the rule, and I don't think it says much about either model. Our HR check says to fail a request that holds "health or medical information about anyone". Is a free flu vaccination for two offices health information about anyone? Our rule didn't say. So the two models read it differently, and one added sentence gave 8 of 8 on both.

We recorded a three-minute video of this on our demo site, on CogniRunner 1.34.0. What follows is my own run of the same procedure on our test site, with the output as it printed. I did three of the steps through an API where you will click: my tokens came from our test hook, I saved the sentence through Jira's workflow REST API, and I switched the model through the test hook. The video shows those screens, and I give the timestamp at each step.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lMpvV03upQA

[!NOTE]
Prerequisites

  • A Jira Cloud site with CogniRunner 1.34.0 or later. The Marketplace calls that build 7.16.0, released 12 October 2026. I ran a development build of 1.34.0 on our test site.
  • An AI provider saved in CogniRunner's Settings. Mine was OpenRouter with openai/gpt-6-luna as the model for validators and rules. If you haven't set one up, the provider tutorial covers it.
  • A company-managed project whose workflow has a CogniRunner AI validator on one transition. Mine was called Send for Review.
  • An email and API token for Jira's REST API. The script reads the published workflow. I ran it as a Jira admin.
  • A CogniRunner admin, to create the REST API token in step 2.
  • Node 18 or later. I used Node v24.15.0. The script has no dependencies.

The video runs on our demo site with issue keys PPL-13 to PPL-27, and my run has COGTEST-3049 to COGTEST-3056 with the same eight texts. Its script takes flags and runs four requests at a time, while the one printed here takes environment variables and runs one at a time. In the video the first round is 7 of 8. Mine was 6 of 8.

[[steps]]

  1. Build the golden dataset — eight requests in a Jira filter, each labelled expect-pass or expect-block.
  2. Create a token — Settings, the card titled Tokens for CogniRunner's REST API.
  3. Save the script — it reads the saved rule from Jira and calls the rule test for each request.
  4. Run the baseline — the site's own model, three rounds.
  5. Run the candidate — one variable, and the site's model stays as it is.
  6. Read the mismatch — decide whether the model or the rule is wrong.
  7. Try the sentence, save it, run both again — first unsaved, then saved.
  8. Switch the site's model — and find the switch and the tests in the audit log.
What one rule test does: one field, one prompt, nothing written

A CogniRunner AI validator sits on a workflow transition. Somebody moves the request. The app sends one field of it (here the Description) to the model together with the prompt you saved. Back comes pass or fail, with a reason. Atlassian's Forge validator module is what carries it: "Validators check that any input made to the transition is valid before the transition is performed."

You may know the Test button in the rule editor. CogniRunner's Rules REST API has the same thing as a call: POST ?resource=rules&action=test. Our docs describe it like this: "the issue is read, the AI answers, and nothing is written." The body carries the issue key, the field and the prompt. Because the prompt travels in the body, you can try a wording before you save it.

An admin token can add ai: {provider, model} to that body, and then this one request runs on another model of a provider the site already has a key for. From the same page: "Nothing is saved or cached: the site's provider, models and keys stay as they were, and the next request without ai runs on the site's provider."

So the whole procedure is a loop over a filter. The same call takes other kinds of rule as well, and I tested validators. The rest of this API is in the release post for Marketplace version 3.3.0 and on the product page. Another thing you can do to the same validator is hand it a document, and the tutorial on giving one an API spec covers that.

Step 1. Build the golden dataset: a Jira filter of 8 labelled issues

People who test LLM apps call a fixed set of inputs with known right answers a golden dataset. PromptLayer's glossary defines the practice as "re-running a golden dataset whenever you change a prompt, model, or workflow to catch quality regressions early." For a validator the right answer is one of two words, so the dataset can live in Jira as plain issues.

Create eight requests in the project the validator guards. Give each the label gate-test, and then expect-pass or expect-block. Mine were four of each:

Key Label Request What decides it COGTEST-3049 expect-pass Onboarding: new hire Freya Nilsson, Security Engineer band, salary, laptop, nothing about health COGTEST-3050 expect-block Salary adjustment: Nora Achterberg, Finance Ops "she was in hospital for a week in August" COGTEST-3051 expect-block Relocation support: Arjun Mehta, Bangalore to Lisbon cleared to fly "after the knee operation" COGTEST-3052 expect-pass Parental leave cover: Lina Haddad, Platform support parental leave, which isn't an illness COGTEST-3053 expect-pass Wellbeing budget: Design team, 2027 standing desks and a gym benefit for 12 people COGTEST-3054 expect-block Relocation allowance: Tomasz Wierzbicki, Kraków to Lisbon "his daughter's asthma" COGTEST-3055 expect-block Reduced hours: Amara Okafor, 32 to 28 hours "a phased return after her burnout absence" COGTEST-3056 expect-pass Flu vaccination: office programme, November 2026 free and optional, for everyone in two offices

All of these people are made up. They belong to the fictional company on our demo site, and the eight are ours. Write yours from requests your own people sent, with the names changed.

Then save the search as a filter. Mine is called Gate tests: HR health check, with this JQL:

project = COGTEST AND labels = gate-test ORDER BY key ASC

Note the filter's id from its URL. Mine was 12450.

Check: the filter should show 8 of 8, and each row should show its expect label. If a row shows another label first, remove the extra labels. Jira sorts labels by name, and in our video session a label called benefits pushed two verdicts behind a +2.

Is eight enough? Probably not for a rule that matters a lot. Traceloop's guide suggests "20-30 'golden set' examples that cover common use cases and known failure modes." Our eight came out of 28 candidates. Our video session ran those 28 on both models, 600 dry runs in all. It kept the ones whose verdict stayed the same over four or five rounds, plus one request where the two models disagreed each time. Four of the dropped ones flipped in 1 round of 3 (a newborn added to a health plan, a return from maternity leave, and two more). A request that flips by itself will fail your test on days when nothing changed, so I'd keep those out of the gate and in a separate list to watch.

Step 2. Create a token for CogniRunner's REST API

Open CogniRunner's admin page, go to the Settings tab and find the card titled Tokens for CogniRunner's REST API. It opens on Viewer and Their own rules. Change those to Admin and Everyone's rules. My tokens had both, and I haven't tried a narrower one. Type a name and click Create token. You see the value once, so copy it now, and copy the Endpoint from the same card. The video shows this card at 0:34, with its two tokens already made.

Our docs put the rule test at editor, and the same call with ai at "admin token + live admin minter". By minter they mean the person who created the token, who must still be an admin when the call arrives. So an editor token should be enough for step 4, going by the docs and the code.

Tokens run out. On the card it says "New tokens expire after 90 days", and mine, created on 13 October, showed an expiry of 11 January 2027. Also treat the endpoint address as private too. It's a Forge web trigger, and Atlassian's page on those says "You should keep these URLs secure." CogniRunner asks for the bearer token on top. I still mask the address everywhere, this page included.

Put the values in your shell:

export JIRA_SITE=https://wolfaenpak.atlassian.net JIRA_EMAIL= JIRA_API_TOKEN=
export RULES_API_URL= RULES_API_TOKEN=cgr_
export WORKFLOW="Software Simplified Workflow for Project COGTEST" TRANSITION="Send for Review" FILTER=12450

That first value is our test site, so put your own there. WORKFLOW is the workflow's name as Jira's workflow list shows it. You'll know whether the token works from the first line the script prints in step 4, which should show its role.

Step 3. Call the Rules REST API to test the Jira workflow validator on each issue

Save this as gate-test.mjs. It needs no packages. savedRule reads the published workflow from Jira and pulls the validator's prompt and field out of the transition. It reads Jira because the rules resource of CogniRunner's REST API has no call that returns a tracked rule's saved prompt in full. testSet reads the filter and takes the expected verdict from the label. runOne posts one request to the rule test and waits if the token's allowance is spent.

#!/usr/bin/env node
// gate-test.mjs: run a CogniRunner AI validator's SAVED prompt over a labelled Jira test set. Node 18+, no dependencies.
// Every call is a dry run (POST ?resource=rules&action=test): the issue is read, the AI answers, nothing is written.
//   JIRA_SITE=https://you.atlassian.net JIRA_EMAIL=... JIRA_API_TOKEN=... \
//   RULES_API_URL= RULES_API_TOKEN=cgr_... \
//   WORKFLOW="" TRANSITION="Send for Review" FILTER= node gate-test.mjs
// Optional: CANDIDATE_MODEL=/ runs each request on that model instead (needs an ADMIN token; the
//   site's own model is not changed). CANDIDATE_PROVIDER defaults to openrouter. ADD_SENTENCE="..." appends one
//   sentence to the saved prompt for this run only, so you can try a wording before you save it.
const E = process.env;
for (const k of ["JIRA_SITE", "JIRA_EMAIL", "JIRA_API_TOKEN", "RULES_API_URL", "RULES_API_TOKEN", "WORKFLOW", "FILTER"]) if (!E[k]) { console.error(`Set ${k}`); process.exit(2); }
const TRANSITION = E.TRANSITION || "Send for Review";
const JAUTH = "Basic " + Buffer.from(`${E.JIRA_EMAIL}:${E.JIRA_API_TOKEN}`).toString("base64");
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));
const pad = (s, n) => String(s ?? "").padEnd(n).slice(0, n);

async function jira(path, body) {
  const r = await fetch(E.JIRA_SITE + path, { method: "POST", headers: { Authorization: JAUTH, Accept: "application/json", "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify(body) });
  if (!r.ok) throw new Error(`Jira ${path}: ${r.status} ${(await r.text()).slice(0, 200)}`);
  return r.json();
}
async function rules(method, query, body) {
  const r = await fetch(`${E.RULES_API_URL}?${query}`, { method, headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${E.RULES_API_TOKEN}`, "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: body ? JSON.stringify(body) : undefined });
  const text = await r.text(); let json = null; try { json = JSON.parse(text); } catch { /* not JSON */ }
  return { status: r.status, json, retryAfter: Number(r.headers.get("retry-after") || 0) };
}

// 1. The rule as SAVED: the CogniRunner validator on the transition, read from the published workflow.
async function savedRule() {
  const j = await jira("/rest/api/3/workflows", { workflowNames: [E.WORKFLOW] });
  for (const w of j.workflows || []) for (const t of w.transitions || []) {
    if (t.name !== TRANSITION) continue;
    for (const v of t.validators || []) {
      if (!/ai-text-field-validator/.test(v.parameters?.key || "")) continue;
      const c = JSON.parse(v.parameters.config);
      return { prompt: c.prompt, fieldId: c.fieldId || "description", enableTools: c.enableTools === true, version: w.version?.versionNumber };
    }
  }
  throw new Error(`No CogniRunner AI validator on "${TRANSITION}" in workflow "${E.WORKFLOW}"`);
}
// 2. The test set: every issue in the filter; the expected verdict is its label.
async function testSet() {
  const j = await jira("/rest/api/3/search/jql", { jql: `filter = ${E.FILTER} ORDER BY key ASC`, fields: ["summary", "labels"], maxResults: 100 });
  return (j.issues || []).map((i) => ({ key: i.key, expected: i.fields.labels.includes("expect-block") ? "BLOCK" : i.fields.labels.includes("expect-pass") ? "PASS" : "?" }))
    .sort((a, b) => Number(a.key.split("-")[1]) - Number(b.key.split("-")[1]));
}
// 3. One dry run through the test door. A 429 means the token's AI allowance is spent: wait for Retry-After.
async function runOne(rule, prompt, issue) {
  const body = { kind: "validation", issueKey: issue.key, prompt, fieldId: rule.fieldId, enableTools: rule.enableTools };
  if (E.CANDIDATE_MODEL) body.ai = { provider: E.CANDIDATE_PROVIDER || "openrouter", model: E.CANDIDATE_MODEL };
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt++) {
    const t0 = Date.now(); const r = await rules("POST", "resource=rules&action=test", body);
    if (r.status === 429) { const s = r.retryAfter || 60; console.error(`  429 on ${issue.key}: allowance spent, waiting ${s} s`); await sleep(s * 1000); continue; }
    if (r.status === 202) return { ...issue, verdict: "QUEUED", seconds: 0, servedBy: "", reason: `self-hosted provider: poll ${r.json.poll}` };
    const res = r.json?.result || {};
    const verdict = r.status !== 200 ? `HTTP ${r.status}` : res.success && res.isValid === true ? "PASS" : res.success && res.isValid === false ? "BLOCK" : "NOT JUDGED";
    return { ...issue, verdict, seconds: Math.round((Date.now() - t0) / 100) / 10, servedBy: r.json?.ai?.servedBy?.map((s) => s.model).join(",") || res.modelUsed || "",
      reason: res.reason || res.error || r.json?.error || "" };
  }
  return { ...issue, verdict: "GAVE UP", seconds: 0, servedBy: "", reason: "429 four times" };
}

const who = await rules("GET", "resource=whoami");
if (who.status !== 200) { console.error(`whoami: HTTP ${who.status} ${who.json?.error || ""}`); process.exit(1); }
const spend = who.json.aiSpend || {};
console.log(`Token role: ${who.json.effective?.role} · AI actions used ${spend.window?.used}/${spend.window?.limit} in this 10-minute window, ${spend.today?.actions}/${spend.today?.limit} today`);
const rule = await savedRule();
const prompt = E.ADD_SENTENCE ? `${rule.prompt} ${E.ADD_SENTENCE.trim()}` : rule.prompt;
const set = await testSet();
console.log(`Rule: ${E.WORKFLOW} · ${TRANSITION} · reads ${rule.fieldId} · workflow version ${rule.version}`);
console.log(`Prompt (${E.ADD_SENTENCE ? "saved + one sentence, this run only" : "as saved"}): ${prompt}`);
console.log(`Model: ${E.CANDIDATE_MODEL ? `${E.CANDIDATE_MODEL} (these requests only; the site's model is not changed)` : "the site's own model"}`);
console.log(`\n${pad("KEY", 13)} ${pad("EXPECTED", 8)} ${pad("VERDICT", 10)} ${pad("SECS", 5)} ${pad("SERVED BY", 28)} REASON`);
let match = 0, slowest = 0;
for (const issue of set) {   // one at a time: calls in parallel made the model slower and one timed out
  const r = await runOne(rule, prompt, issue); const ok = r.verdict === r.expected; if (ok) match++; slowest = Math.max(slowest, r.seconds);
  console.log(`${pad(r.key, 13)} ${pad(r.expected, 8)} ${pad(r.verdict + (ok ? "" : " ✗"), 10)} ${pad(r.seconds, 5)} ${pad(r.servedBy, 28)} ${r.verdict === "PASS" ? "" : r.reason}`);
}
console.log(`\n${match} of ${set.length} match · slowest ${slowest} s`);
process.exit(match === set.length ? 0 : 1);

Why one request at a time? In the video session, four calls in flight pushed the site's model to 16.1 seconds. With eight in flight, one call ran past 20 seconds and came back as a timeout. My first run's eight calls added up to about 26 seconds, which I can live with.

It exits 0 when all verdicts match and 1 when one doesn't, so the same file works as a step in CI.

Check: open a new terminal, where the variables from step 2 aren't set, and run node gate-test.mjs there. It should print Set JIRA_SITE and stop, which tells you Node found the file and nothing was called.

Step 4. Run the LLM regression testing baseline on the site's model

With the variables from step 2 exported:

node gate-test.mjs

Token role: admin · AI actions used 0/20 in this 10-minute window, 0/200 today
Rule: Software Simplified Workflow for Project COGTEST · Send for Review · reads description · workflow version 1079
Prompt (as saved): Fail it if it contains health or medical information about anyone: an illness, injury, surgery, sick leave, diagnosis or treatment. This is an HR request a manager sends to People Ops for approval. When it fails, say in one short sentence which detail must be removed. Otherwise it passes.
Model: the site's own model

KEY           EXPECTED VERDICT    SECS  SERVED BY                    REASON
COGTEST-3049  PASS     PASS       3.5   openai/gpt-6-luna            
COGTEST-3050  BLOCK    BLOCK      2.8   openai/gpt-6-luna            Remove the detail that Nora was in hospital for a week in August.
COGTEST-3051  BLOCK    BLOCK      2.5   openai/gpt-6-luna            Remove the detail that his physiotherapist cleared him to fly after knee surgery.
COGTEST-3052  PASS     BLOCK ✗    2.6   openai/gpt-6-luna            Remove the detail that Lina Haddad is on parental leave.
COGTEST-3053  PASS     PASS       2.9   openai/gpt-6-luna            
COGTEST-3054  BLOCK    BLOCK      2.9   openai/gpt-6-luna            Remove the detail that his daughter’s asthma is worse in Kraków’s winters.
COGTEST-3055  BLOCK    BLOCK      3.7   openai/gpt-6-luna            Remove the detail about her burnout absence and phased return.
COGTEST-3056  PASS     BLOCK ✗    4.7   openai/gpt-6-luna            Remove the detail about offering flu vaccinations through the occupational health provider.

6 of 8 match · slowest 4.7 s

Check: the first line should show Token role: admin (or editor), the Rule line should show your transition and reads description, and the Prompt line should be your saved prompt word for word. Under SERVED BY you see the model that answered.

So that's two misses. I ran the same command twice more and got 7 of 8 both times. All three rounds blocked the flu vaccination, each time with a different sentence ("Remove the detail about free flu vaccination, which is medical information." was round two). Parental leave was blocked in the first round and passed in the next two.

If I'd stopped after one run I would have gone off to fix parental leave, which was right two times out of three. So run the baseline at least three times and sort the misses into stable ones and flaky ones before you touch anything. Here the stable one is COGTEST-3056.

Watch the allowance while you do. A token gets 20 AI actions per 10 minutes, and three rounds of eight are 24. I used a new token for each pair of rounds. With one token, the script is written to wait out the Retry-After the API sends (I never let it get that far, so I haven't watched it do so).

Step 5. Switch from OpenAI's model to Claude for one request, not the whole site

Same command, one more variable:

CANDIDATE_MODEL=anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 node gate-test.mjs

Token role: admin · AI actions used 8/20 in this 10-minute window, 8/200 today
Rule: Software Simplified Workflow for Project COGTEST · Send for Review · reads description · workflow version 1079
Prompt (as saved): Fail it if it contains health or medical information about anyone: an illness, injury, surgery, sick leave, diagnosis or treatment. This is an HR request a manager sends to People Ops for approval. When it fails, say in one short sentence which detail must be removed. Otherwise it passes.
Model: anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 (these requests only; the site's model is not changed)

KEY           EXPECTED VERDICT    SECS  SERVED BY                    REASON
COGTEST-3049  PASS     PASS       3.2   anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   
COGTEST-3050  BLOCK    BLOCK      3     anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   Remove the sentence stating that Nora was in hospital for a week in August, as it discloses medical information.
COGTEST-3051  BLOCK    BLOCK      3.8   anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   Remove the reference to the knee operation and physiotherapist clearance, which is medical information about an employee.
COGTEST-3052  PASS     PASS       4.5   anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   
COGTEST-3053  PASS     PASS       3     anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   
COGTEST-3054  BLOCK    BLOCK      4.5   anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   Remove the reference to the daughter's asthma, since it is a medical condition about a family member.
COGTEST-3055  BLOCK    BLOCK      3.1   anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   Remove the reference to her burnout absence and occupational health involvement, as these disclose medical or health information about an employee.
COGTEST-3056  PASS     PASS       7.4   anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   

8 of 8 match · slowest 7.4 s

Check: the Model line should show "these requests only", and SERVED BY should show the candidate on all eight rows. Then open CogniRunner's Settings. You should see the model for validators and rules still set to the one you started with.

Both models here are reached through OpenRouter. For eight requests the model id changed, and the site's provider didn't change at all. To try a model through another provider, say Anthropic directly, that provider needs a key saved in Settings first. A request can't bring one. I tried sending an apiKey in the body and got a 400 that says so (it's in the troubleshooting list).

I picked the candidate id by reading OpenRouter's models API that morning. anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 was the newest Claude Haiku id on it, listed as created on 7 October 2026. I compared the two models as models a few days ago, and this page isn't a second round of that. Eight requests on one prompt is far too little to rank anybody, and I ran the candidate on the unfixed rule once.

Step 6. Read the mismatch: the rule did not say what HR meant

Here is the Description of the request the site's model kept blocking:

Change: free flu vaccination for everyone in the Lisbon and Berlin offices, run by our occupational health provider on 18 and 19 November; budget 1,950 EUR for up to 150 people.
Effective date: 18 November 2026
Approver: Ines Kowalczyk (Head of People)
Reason: it is optional and no one's answers or records come to People Ops; last year 96 people took part.

And the rule says to fail a request that holds "health or medical information about anyone: an illness, injury, surgery, sick leave, diagnosis or treatment". A vaccination is a treatment. Read literally, the site's model has a case.

What did HR mean, though? They want to stop a manager typing somebody's hospital stay into an approval request. GDPR's definition of data concerning health is "personal data related to the physical or mental health of a natural person, including the provision of health care services, which reveal information about his or her health status". A vaccination is a health care service. But a programme open to 150 people, with no list of who went, reveals nobody's health status. That reading is mine and I'm no lawyer, but it's the one our People Ops example is built on.

The rule left room for both readings, and I think each model took one. Swapping the model would have hidden that, and the next model update could bring it back.

Our video session tried three sentences before the one that worked. Sentence one fixed the flu request and tipped a return from maternity leave into a block. That happened in all 3 runs on the site's model and 1 of 3 on the candidate. Sentence two named parental and maternity leave outright and made the site's model worse (it scored 4 and 5 of 8). Sentence three left a burnout-risk request wrong in 2 runs of 2. Traceloop's guide has a line for this: "A simple wording change can dramatically alter an LLM's performance, fixing one issue while silently creating another." So after an edit I run all eight again.

This one held:

A benefit, programme or budget for a whole team is not health information about anyone; only a detail about a named person's or a relative's illness, injury or treatment is.
Step 7. Run prompt regression testing after the one-sentence fix

Try the sentence before saving it. ADD_SENTENCE appends it to the saved prompt for this run, and the workflow isn't touched:

ADD_SENTENCE="A benefit, programme or budget for a whole team is not health information about anyone; only a detail about a named person's or a relative's illness, injury or treatment is." node gate-test.mjs

Token role: admin · AI actions used 0/20 in this 10-minute window, 0/200 today
Rule: Software Simplified Workflow for Project COGTEST · Send for Review · reads description · workflow version 1079
Prompt (saved + one sentence, this run only): Fail it if it contains health or medical information about anyone: an illness, injury, surgery, sick leave, diagnosis or treatment. This is an HR request a manager sends to People Ops for approval. When it fails, say in one short sentence which detail must be removed. Otherwise it passes. A benefit, programme or budget for a whole team is not health information about anyone; only a detail about a named person's or a relative's illness, injury or treatment is.
Model: the site's own model

KEY           EXPECTED VERDICT    SECS  SERVED BY                    REASON
COGTEST-3049  PASS     PASS       3.7   openai/gpt-6-luna            
COGTEST-3050  BLOCK    BLOCK      3.3   openai/gpt-6-luna            Remove the detail that Nora was in hospital for a week in August.
COGTEST-3051  BLOCK    BLOCK      4     openai/gpt-6-luna            Remove the detail that his physiotherapist cleared him to fly only after the knee operation.
COGTEST-3052  PASS     PASS       4.7   openai/gpt-6-luna            
COGTEST-3053  PASS     PASS       3.7   openai/gpt-6-luna            
COGTEST-3054  BLOCK    BLOCK      3.3   openai/gpt-6-luna            Remove the detail that his daughter’s asthma is worse in Kraków’s winters.
COGTEST-3055  BLOCK    BLOCK      2.8   openai/gpt-6-luna            Remove the detail about her burnout absence and phased return agreed with occupational health.
COGTEST-3056  PASS     PASS       4     openai/gpt-6-luna            

8 of 8 match · slowest 4.7 s

Two more rounds on the site's model gave 8 of 8 again. So did one round with CANDIDATE_MODEL set.

Then save it. In Jira's workflow editor, open the transition, expand its validators, open the CogniRunner validator, add the sentence at the end of the Validation prompt, click Update and then Update workflow. The video does this at 1:32. In our session's notes the saved rule carried the new prompt at once, so treat it as live for the next person who moves a request. To undo it, take the sentence out the same way. The session put the old prompt back between takes.

Run both commands once more, without ADD_SENTENCE:

node gate-test.mjs
CANDIDATE_MODEL=anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 node gate-test.mjs

The last line of each, as mine printed:

8 of 8 match · slowest 3.5 s
8 of 8 match · slowest 5.1 s

Check: the Rule line should show the workflow version one higher (mine went from 1079 to 1080). Its Prompt line should show "as saved" and end with the new sentence.

Step 8. Switch the site's model and read the audit log

In Settings, set the model for validators and rules to the candidate and click Save models (2:28 in the video). Then run the plain command again:

node gate-test.mjs

Model: the site's own model

8 of 8 match · slowest 9.4 s

Those are the Model line and the last line. SERVED BY read anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 on all eight rows with no CANDIDATE_MODEL set. That 9.4 seconds was the slowest call of the morning.

Open the Audit log and search for your provider's name.

Check: you should see a row labelled AI model changed that reads "Set the OpenRouter model to anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 (was openai/gpt-6-luna)." Under it there's one row per candidate test: "Tested a validator on COGTEST-3056 with OpenRouter (anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5), 1 AI call; the site's own provider was not changed."

You get a row for each test that ran on another model, and none for tests on the site's own model. I counted: 24 rows for the 24 candidate tests (three rounds of eight) plus one for my wrong model id, and nothing for the 84 dry runs that named no other model (seven rounds of eight on gpt-6-luna, the one after the switch, and 20 calls I made to find where the allowance stops). That makes sense to me. A test on another model sends issue text somewhere the site doesn't normally send it, and that's the thing an auditor would ask about.

Those rows name the issue because of this exercise, by the way. When the video session first ran it on 1.33.5, eight tests in a row produced eight identical audit rows and you couldn't tell which request's text had gone out. Back then a token's usage also counted zero AI tokens for validator tests, and the token card's title mentioned listeners and scheduled jobs but said nothing of rules. Those were three bugs of ours, and 1.34.0 fixes them.

Run the set more than once: one verdict flipped in 1 of 3 rounds

I don't think a model that gives a different answer on the same text breaks the test, but you need to know it's happening. On the rule as saved, the parental leave request flipped in 1 of my 3 rounds. With the sentence it passed in all 4 of my rounds on the site's model (three unsaved, one saved). In the video session's files the same request, with the sentence, was wrong once in 13 calls on the site's model. That one miss arrived during a recording. They threw the take away. Across every request they tried with the sentence, the eight and the dropped candidates, the site's model was right in 163 of 164 calls.

One more thing a matching verdict doesn't tell you. The site's model blocked the reduced-hours request in all seven of its rounds, which matches the label. In two of them the reason named the wrong person, and one of those read "Remove the detail about Priya Raman’s burnout absence and phased return." The request is Amara Okafor's. Priya Raman is the approver. My script compares PASS and BLOCK and never reads the sentence, so it scored that as a match. If the wording of the refusal matters to you (it's what the person sees on the transition), read the REASON column yourself now and then.

Langfuse's write-up splits checks into "exact-match or deterministic assertions for structured outputs and business rules, and semantic evaluation when valid answers can differ in wording." A verdict against a label is the first kind. Judging the reason sentence would be the second kind, and this script doesn't attempt it.

If it didn't work

I sent each of these on purpose and got these answers from the API on 1.34.0.

What I sent What came back A bearer value that isn't a CogniRunner token HTTP 401 {"error":"unauthorized"} The 21st AI action on one token inside one 10-minute window HTTP 429, Retry-After: 218, "This API token has started 20 AI actions (listener tests, job runs, agent ticks, agent uploads) in the last 10 minutes, which is its limit. Try again in 218 seconds." ai: {provider: "claude"} HTTP 400 Unknown AI provider "claude". Name one of: openai, azure, openrouter, anthropic, lmstudio, compatible, ollama, goose, atlassian, bedrock, gemini. ai for Anthropic on a site with no Anthropic key HTTP 409 No Anthropic key is saved on this site, so nothing was sent. ai carrying apiKey HTTP 400, reason key-not-accepted A model id OpenRouter doesn't serve HTTP 200, with AI error (400): anthropic/claude-haiku-9.9 is not a valid model ID inside the result No prompt in the body HTTP 400, reason bad-request, with missing: ["prompt"]

You'll meet the 429 first. A token gets 20 AI actions per 10 minutes and 200 a day. One round of 8 on each model is 16, so a third round inside the same window hits the limit. That window follows the clock: a token of mine that showed 16 used at 07:19 showed 0 at 07:23, after the :20 mark. For the app's other meter, see the rate limit tutorial.

Be careful with a wrong model id, because the HTTP status is 200. For that answer the script prints NOT JUDGED and counts a mismatch. It still took one AI action and wrote one audit row, which is the row you can see in the screenshot above.

If savedRule throws on JSON.parse, look at how your validator's config is stored in the workflow. It was plain JSON on both sites I read. I haven't checked a very large config.

What this set doesn't test

A validator reads one field. Mine reads Description, so a hospital stay typed into a comment or an attachment goes straight past it. Treat the check as a quality gate before HR approves. I wouldn't call it a security control.

A dry run takes as long as the model takes. A live transition allows 20 seconds. With a hosted provider like OpenRouter, a check that gets no answer in that time lets the transition through and the execution log says so. Self-hosted providers are different (LM Studio, Ollama, Goose Swarm or an OpenAI-compatible server). For those, 1.34.0 added a hold you can turn on. It refuses the transition while the check finishes in the background, and it's off by default. My slowest dry run was 9.4 seconds, so neither case came up. On a self-hosted provider the rule test answers with a task to poll, and this script prints QUEUED for that and doesn't poll.

I didn't make a real transition on this run. Our video session did, on 12 October, on the demo site. There the site's model blocked a copy of the flu request in the test and answered 400 on the real transition. With the candidate set, the test passed and the request moved for real. So I have one pair, a day old.

Jira has nothing like this built in that I could find. Atlassian has an evaluation feature for Rovo agents that takes a CSV of up to 100 prompts. It's for agents. Jira's nearest open request that I know of, JRACLOUD-98947, had 3 votes when I read it on 13 October.

What you have now

[[takeaways]]

  • A Jira filter that is your validator's test set: eight requests, each labelled with the verdict you expect.
  • An 80-line script that reads the saved rule from Jira, dry-runs it on each request and exits 1 on a mismatch.
  • A way to run the same set on another model with one variable and an admin token, while the site stays on its model.
  • A way to try a sentence with ADD_SENTENCE before you save it into the workflow.
  • An audit row for each test that ran on another model, naming the issue, and one for the switch.
  • A baseline you ran three times, so you know which misses are stable.

If you're about to change the model behind a rule people depend on, I'd build the eight requests today and run the baseline before reading anything else about the new model. And if the script is going to call a Forge app from CI for more than a test, the OAuth 2.0 tutorial shows the other way in.

items.title: 66% of billion-dollar companies leave critical bugs unpatched — the part the AI bug-hunting hype leaves out
items.summary: Chainguard has launched an AI-powered security harness that uses frontier models, including Anthropic’s restricted Claude Mythos 5.1, to find and fix exploitable vulnerabilities in application code that conventional scanners miss. Developers can use Chainguard Harness without direct access to Mythos, but the company hasn’t disclosed which models handle vulnerability discovery for those customers. The company says Harness has found serious vulnerabilities in codebases that had already undergone extensive security scanning, including software used in critical infrastructure. Details about the affected projects, the flaws themselves, and their remediation status remain undisclosed. Announced Wednesday, Harness leads a four-product launch alongside Workspaces, Checks, and expanded Libraries protections, extending Chainguard’s reach beyond hardened container images and dependencies into agent execution environments and CI verification. Mythos access without Glasswing Anthropic has restricted Claude Mythos 5.1 access to organizations participating in Project Glasswing , leaving open which models Harness customers outside the program will use. Harness will also be available through Anthropic’s Claude Marketplace, allowing teams to use existing Anthropic spending commitments rather than secure a separate budget. The AI exploit gap The launches come alongside The AI Exploit Gap , a Chainguard-commissioned Wakefield Research survey of 1,300 security leaders across nine markets. More than half said their organizations knowingly leave high or critical vulnerabilities unpatched at least sometimes, with the figure reaching 66% at companies with $1 billion or more in revenue, compared with 27% at companies below $250 million. “AI can find and chain flaws in minutes, while fixing them still moves at human speed and competes with product deadlines and uptime,” Quincy Castro, Chainguard’s chief information security officer, said in a statement. “Patching faster isn’t viable for most folks, and it will consume increasing amounts of resources just to keep pace.” “AI can find and chain flaws in minutes, while fixing them still moves at human speed and competes with product deadlines and uptime” Isolated microVMs for agents Each developer and coding agent gets a hardware-isolated microVM with network policies that restrict access to internal systems. Credentials stay outside the agent’s environment, limiting what a compromised agent or malicious dependency can reach. Signed activity logs record what each agent did so teams can keep an audit trail across multiple autonomous sessions. CI inside the agent loop Chainguard Checks lets coding agents run CI checks directly during development and receive signed results in seconds. Agents can run tests, inspect failures, and revise code before opening a pull request, avoiding the CI queues that become harder to manage as vendors like Cognition, Microsoft, and Augment Code turn coding agents into shared team infrastructure running multiple sessions in parallel. To avoid rebuilding environments on every run, Checks uses warm snapshots with dependencies already installed and refreshes them in the background when the lockfile changes. Each workflow step runs in a separate hardware-isolated microVM built from Chainguard OS packages, including FIPS-compliant toolchains. With Workspaces, agent sessions pause during verification and resume with structured failure logs in context. With Workspaces, agent sessions pause during verification and resume with structured failure logs in context. Runners never hold long-lived credentials. Instead, a host-side proxy injects short-lived credentials into outbound requests, while declarative egress policies restrict network access and can terminate a microVM if it attempts an unauthorized connection. Successful runs produce signed attestations tied to the execution environment, test results, and commit, which merge gates can verify without rerunning the suite. Checks is available now in beta. Libraries Lock Down Late-Breaking Bugs Chainguard Libraries is adding secure package endpoints for Go and .NET, along with CVE remediation for JavaScript, and Go. Java and Python support will also expand to cover newly disclosed vulnerabilities discovered through AI-assisted research, including flaws in dependencies that coding agents may have already pulled into a project. Chainguard Libraries is adding secure package endpoints for Go and .NET, along with CVE remediation for JavaScript, and Go. The changes build on Chainguard Repository , a policy-enforced endpoint for open source dependencies, and its partnership with Cursor , allowing coding agents to resolve packages through Chainguard’s catalog instead of pulling directly from public registries.

items.title: Evidence Ledger Boosts Multimodal Reasoning by Up to 15%
items.summary: Replacing raw dialogue with an explicit evidence ledger lifts multimodal reasoning quality by roughly ten to fifteen percent. The gain comes from swapping the unwieldy full‑context transcript for a compact, query‑driven list of observations that the agent can re‑inject on demand. This shift turns the conversation into a focused retrieval loop rather than a passive scroll through hours of video and audio. Until now, most multimodal agents fed the entire audio‑visual sequence straight into the language model at each turn. The approach relied on massive context windows and hoped the transformer would implicitly discover relevant snippets. Those methods struggled with long videos because token budgets were exhausted before any reasoning could happen, and they offered no guarantee that cross‑modal evidence was actually consulted. Adaptive Multi‑modal Agentic Reasoning introduces a structured evidence ledger that replaces the full dialogue history and delivers a 16.3 % absolute lift on the MMOU benchmark over the base Qwen3‑Omni‑Instruct model. “On benchmarks featuring long-form video lengths, such as MMOU and LVOmni, OmniSeek achieves 70.4% and 44.2%, outperforming the base Qwen3-Omni-Instruct by margins of +16.3% and +8.4%, respectively.” [1] The ledger is populated by a policy that decides when to look or listen, extracts short audio or visual clips, and appends only those slices back into the context. Because the token footprint stays constant, the model can iterate more reasoning steps within the same budget, which translates directly into higher downstream scores across several datasets. The paper’s gains are tied to its two‑stage reinforcement‑learning pipeline, which introduces additional optimization steps beyond the initial supervised pretraining. Moreover, the reported improvements focus on long‑form video tasks; it remains unclear whether the same ledger‑centric design would help on short clips or purely textual multimodal prompts. This suggests that the evidence ledger’s benefit might be bounded by the presence of rich, temporally extended signals and by the availability of a well‑engineered RL setup. If the observed 10–15 % lift holds across real‑world deployments, benchmark suites for multimodal reasoning should replace raw transcript baselines with an explicit evidence‑ledger protocol as the new default. Model developers can adopt the ledger interface without expanding token limits, gaining higher accuracy simply by making evidence acquisition a first‑class step in the reasoning loop. The field will likely see a rapid shift toward tool‑augmented agents that treat observation retrieval as a controllable resource rather than an implicit side effect. References OmniSeek: Native Tool Integration for Multi-turn Audio-Visual Reasoning

items.title: Google Play Lets US Users Build Personal Android Apps in AI Studio Without a Developer Account
items.summary: Google is rolling out an update to Google Play that lets users build personal Android apps with Google AI Studio and install them on their own phone using a standard Google account, according to an announcement on the Google blog. The feature is available starting today in the United States for users aged 18 and older. Google describes the process as "vibe coding" personal projects, and no developer background is required. The company gives examples such as a custom stat tracker for a local recreational league or a family organizer built around one household's routine. How Personal Apps Work on Google Play The personal app feature removes the steps that normally apply to publishing on Google Play. Users do not need a developer account, do not pay registration fees, and skip the usual publishing steps to get the app onto their device. According to Google, the apps created this way: install only on the creator's own device at launch stay private and separate from the public Google Play catalog can be moved to a professional developer account later if the creator wants a public release Sharing is not part of the first release. Google says that in the coming months users will be able to share personal apps privately with a small circle of friends and family. Users in the US who want to try it can follow these steps once the update reaches their account: Check the phone for the latest Google Play Store update, which Google says begins rolling out today. Build the app in Google AI Studio while signed in with a standard Google account. Deploy the finished app to the phone through Google Play. Open the app from the phone; it stays limited to that device until private sharing arrives. Other Google Play Changes Rolling Out The personal app feature is part of a larger Google Play update. Ask Play can now generate side-by-side comparisons of similar apps, covering key differences and user sentiment, and a feature called Play in Gemini will bring app and game recommendations into Gemini chats soon. On the gaming side, Game Finder builds a "Gamer DNA" profile from how a person plays and their stated preferences, and it is rolling out in the US today. Sprints, available globally, are 48-hour challenges for groups of two to five players, tracked through a new Sidekick in-game overlay that also records 30-second gameplay clips. Titles including Dave the Diver and Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun are arriving on Play with cross-save between Android and PC. Google is also adding a Family Link option that lets parents share a child's general age range with apps instead of more detailed personal data. Personal app creation is limited to adult users in the United States, and Google has not announced when it will expand to additional countries or age groups. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader.

items.summary: Apple has announced the HomeView, the company's first smart display, at a media event in New York City. The HomeView costs $299, preorders are open now, and sales begin November 13 in the US, UK, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, India, Singapore, and South Africa. items.title: Microsoft Forms Xbox Labs to Bring Xbox Games to Web Browsers and New Hardware
items.summary: Microsoft has formed Xbox Labs, a small team of game makers, engineers, and scientists that will turn emerging technology into products for Xbox players and developers, according to a memo from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma published on Xbox Wire on October 13. The announcement puts particular emphasis on web browsers and on getting new and older games onto devices they were never built for. Sharma says she asked Scott to stand up the group. The memo does not list products, release dates, or prices. Why Xbox Is Creating Xbox Labs The memo points to recent community projects as the trigger. In recent weeks, Sharma writes, games have been "rapidly decompiled and rebuilt" to run on hardware they were not designed for. Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run in a browser through WebAssembly and WebGPU, which the memo says is approaching 90% global browser support. Sharma calls these results good for players, "even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models." Xbox Labs is meant to explore the same ideas from inside Microsoft: easier access to games, new life for older titles, and tools that let more players become creators. Xbox Labs is not framed as a pure research group. Its job, per the memo, is to turn emerging ideas into things players and developers can experience. Sharma's memo says Xbox Labs will "build in the open," learn from what players do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating. Microsoft also plans to share the tools it builds with developers across the industry. Sharma ties the effort to AI agents as well. She notes that coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software, and argues games share those properties. According to the memo, people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing Xbox games, about five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide. What Xbox Labs Means for Xbox Players The initiative extends Xbox's backward compatibility work, which started more than a decade ago, and the more recent Disc-to-Digital program that lets players digitize their physical games. It also supports Sharma's goal of reaching 1 billion players per day. Sharma says Xbox's existing priorities are unchanged. The company remains committed to making games, to its hardware, and to acting as a steward of its IP and the communities around it, and Xbox Labs is meant to explore new technology "without abandoning the work already underway." There is nothing for players to install or sign up for yet. Players interested in official browser versions of Xbox or Xbox 360 games should follow Xbox Wire, where the memo was published, for the first Xbox Labs releases. The announcement follows the launch of Xbox XP, an entertainment division for film and TV projects, last week. Microsoft has not said which games Xbox Labs will start with, which platforms beyond the browser it will target, or whether its releases will be free, sold upfront, or supported by in-game purchases or ads. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader.

items.title: Firefox takes aim at the enterprise browser market
items.summary: There’s growing talk of digital sovereignty as enterprises rethink past consolidation decisions made in the name of simplicity. Mozilla, developer of Firefox, argues that a “very specific, very important layer” has been mostly missing from that conversation: The browser. To that end, the company has unveiled Firefox Enterprise in a bid to diversify the browser engine to support privacy, control, and security. The new offering combines the Firefox browser with a management console that enterprises can run on their own infrastructure using their own tooling. Companies get a full view of their data and can govern how it moves, and IT teams can manage policy, access, and set controls around AI use. Firefox is already deployed across thousands of organizations and used by roughly 200 million people each month, Mozilla said. It is built on Mozilla’s independent Gecko engine, the only major browser engine developed outside Google and Apple. “If all your options are built with the same technology underneath, ‘choice’ is a lie. So is control,” Mozilla CEO Anthony Enzor-DeMeo observed in the blog post announcing the product . The promise of Firefox Enterprise “Firefox is hardly the first browser vendor to offer an enterprise-optimized choice,” said independent technology analyst Carmi Levy . “But it carves out a unique value proposition for IT organizations intent on maintaining independent control over how browsers are deployed, configured, secured, and managed.” Firefox Enterprise keeps core management within an organization’s own environment; its data, keys, telemetry, and policy remain in controlled boundaries that the organization can run on-premises and audit itself. IT teams can gate access and control policies based on user and device. They can also export browser events and audit activity in their SIEM, and native DLP helps prevent data loss. Mozilla is particularly gearing Firefox Enterprise to organizations with strict security, governance, and compliance concerns. The offering can help enterprises meet regulatory requirements like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA), the NIS2 directive, ISO27001, and SOC2. IT teams can set external connection controls, allow or block organization-wide add-ons, and restrict browsing with a lockdown mode “so one zero-day doesn’t take down every browser in the estate,” the announcement said. AI use can be allowed, restricted, or disabled. From a security standpoint , enterprises can set data loss prevention (DLP) rules by domain or action, and integrate with existing security information and event management (SIEM) tools like Trellix or Broadcom to extend analysis into the browser. IT teams can protect against phishing, malware, and malicious sites with native isolation, extension control, and managed security updates. Access can be gated based on user and device, without the need for virtual private networks (VPNs), remote browser isolation (RBI), and virtual desktops. The company said that it will use a subscription model “that doesn’t depend on monetizing customer data or forcing a roadmap.” Firefox Enterprise includes Firefox Professional support; for businesses running the free Firefox browser without Firefox Enterprise, Firefox Professional support is available as a paid subscription. Firefox Enterprise is now being introduced in Europe, initially across France, Germany, Austria, and Switzerland, with more markets to follow. Mozilla is also developing Thunderbird Enterprise, which will manage Thunderbird email, calendar, and contacts. The case for enterprise browsers Largely thanks to the shift to cloud-based computing, the browser has evolved from a simple internet gateway to the place where most workers spend virtually all of their time. This makes them “the very epicenters of modern enterprise digital security,” said Levy. Thus it makes sense for IT to consider the merits of a dedicated enterprise browser. But, Levy said, “there are no ideal solutions in IT, and enterprise-class browsers are no exception.” Employees may bristle at additional layers of controls and raise privacy concerns around centralized monitoring. Administrative complexity is also a concern, as existing identity management, endpoint management, monitoring, and data protection tools may not always “cleanly integrate” with a more robust browser, he noted. Enterprise-class browsers also can’t stop “less-than-ideally-trained employees” from clicking on phishing links , and they also can’t protect against “every last malicious extension.” As always, bad actors can find ways to compromise sensitive corporate data or otherwise use AI toolsets in unsanctioned ways. But these types of browser can help minimize AI-related risks as employees lean more heavily into chatbots and agents. Admins can craft more flexible rules of engagement; for example, workers could access a web app for deep-dive analysis, but humans and AI alike could be prevented from copying data externally. Enterprise browsers also allow more granular control of AI features, and even disengagement if they conflict with policy. Key differentiators Firefox Enterprise isn’t the only option when choosing an enterprise browser, however. Microsoft Edge for Business would likely still be the preferred choice for environments already heavily invested in Microsoft’s enterprise Azure and Microsoft 365 ecosystem, Levy pointed out. Similar logic would apply to Google Chrome Enterprise’s appeal for those already committed to Google’s cloud and productivity infrastructure. And the Prisma Browser from Palo Alto Networks integrates aggressive cybersecurity tools with monitoring of AI use, remote devices, and unmanaged devices. Firefox Enterprise’s key differentiation is its use of the Gecko browser engine, and its management console that can be deployed on a company’s own infrastructure, Levy said. This might make it a good fit for shops that want to minimize implementation disruptions to existing data management, access control, and compliance protocols. “Firefox Enterprise lets customers craft their own deployment roadmap, assuming they have the skills and resources to self-manage the process,” Levy said.

items.title: Denmark’s Hackers Didn’t Need Skill, They Needed an AI and a Bad Password
items.summary: A single compromised vendor account just exposed personal records on 8.8 million people, more than Denmark’s entire population, pulled from the country’s national identity register. The attacker says an AI model wrote the program that did it, and a basic coding bug accidentally spared an entire birth year from exposure. What Happened Danish authorities disclosed on October 5 that hackers abused a private company’s legitimate access to the Central Person Register, or CPR, the database that assigns every resident, deceased person, and emigrant a unique identification number. The breach exposed names, addresses, and CPR numbers tied to roughly 8.75 million records, according to figures the attacker provided to Danish newspaper Politiken. That total includes about 5.5 million living people and 3.3 million deceased ones, out of the roughly 11 million records the CPR holds. Denmark’s actual population is about 6 million. The compromised account belonged to Pays ApS, a small Odense-based data services firm that helps business customers verify addresses, deaths, and relocations through CPR lookups. Managing director Sophie Laursen confirmed on October 9 that an external party had misused the company’s authorized access. Between September 10 and September 20, the intruder ran roughly 14 million automated searches, 8.75 million of which returned usable records. Nobody caught it in real time. A ministry staffer discovered the breach on October 2 after noticing an unusually large invoice tied to Pays’s search volume, 12 days after the activity had already stopped. Politiken later reported that at least three Pays accounts, including an administrator account, used the password “123456.” Separately, a person claiming responsibility told the paper, through an encrypted chat conducted in English, that they got in using a leaked password belonging to a former Pays employee. Danish authorities have confirmed neither account of how the attacker got in, nor the attacker’s identity. Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund called the incident “extremely serious” and ordered a review of the CPR system’s security controls. Datatilsynet, Denmark’s data protection authority, and the National Special Crime Unit are both investigating. The attacker also told Politiken that artificial intelligence wrote the extraction program, a script more than 40,000 characters long, saying “any AI model launched within the past year or so would be able to do it.” Two experts who reviewed the code for Politiken agreed it looked AI-generated. The clearest evidence: a bug sent the program searching for people born in 1877 instead of 1977, so the leaked dataset is missing an entire birth year by accident. Why It Matters None of the attacker’s claims, about the password, the AI tooling, or the stated intent not to sell the data, have been independently verified by Danish authorities. But the pattern underneath them is familiar. CPR numbers function in Denmark the way Social Security numbers function in the United States: as both a universal identifier and, in practice, a stand-in for proof of identity. Banks, employers, hospitals, and landlords all request it. Once a number like that leaks at population scale, treating it as a secret stops making sense, because tens of millions of other parties already hold it too. Danish cybersecurity specialist Jan Kaastrup told broadcaster TV 2 that the CPR number’s role as an implicit secret is now simply “broken.” That is also why the discovery method matters as much as the breach itself. Fourteen million automated queries ran over ten days through one vendor account, and nothing in the CPR system’s monitoring flagged it as abnormal. An invoice surfaced the intrusion, not a security alert. The pattern echoes other 2026 incidents, including the Thomson Reuters court-records exposure and a string of vendor-credential breaches across healthcare and law firms, where the attacker broke nothing technical. They simply used access that was already there. The AI detail is the part generating headlines, and it deserves scrutiny rather than alarm. A 40,000-character script that enumerates sequential ID numbers and pulls matching records is not a sophisticated exploit. What AI assistance plausibly did was compress the time and skill needed to write that script from days to minutes, not invent a new attack method. The century bug, mistaking 1977 for 1877, is a two-digit-year error that has dogged software since long before large language models existed, apparently inherited now by the tools that write software today. Our Take: Our take is that the password and the AI detail are the least important facts in this story, even though they are the most quotable. The real failure is structural: a government handed broad, standing search access to a small vendor with no apparent limit on query volume, no real-time anomaly detection, and no requirement for multi-factor protection on an account that could enumerate an entire nation’s population. Fixing the password would not have fixed that. Denmark’s advice to lean on MitID and one-time codes instead of the CPR number is the right move, but it is also an admission that the number itself is now permanently compromised for roughly 8.8 million people. Expect more governments to face this same reckoning as AI tooling keeps lowering the cost of mass-scale enumeration attacks against databases built around a single, static identifier. The institutions that get ahead of it will be the ones that stop treating identity numbers as secrets and start treating vendor access itself as the perimeter worth watching.

items.title: OpenAI says it found a 'hidden' recording device planted in its office
items.summary: OpenAI said it found a recording device "hidden" in one of its offices and reported the matter to the FBI. Bloomberg/Getty Images OpenAI said the device was "concealed in toilet paper" and planted in one of its offices. The company said it then used its own models to determine who planted the device. The Department of Justice said an employee was arrested on October 9. OpenAI said it found a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in one of its offices and used its own AI to identify who planted the device. "We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier," OpenAI wrote in an X post on Tuesday. "We referred the matter to the FBI, and we're grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI's investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work." A statement from the Justice Department said that the employee in question is allegedly 35-year-old Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national. Alfozan was arrested on October 9 and charged with using an electronic device to intercept oral communications. Alfozan made his first appearance in federal court on Tuesday, the statement said. A complaint filed in the Northern District of California said that an employee found a USB device surreptitiously placed on the back of a television located in an " executive conference room ." The device was concealed in toilet paper, the complaint said. Photos attached to the court documents and DOJ statement showed the device positioned behind what appears to be a television. The complaint said the device consists of a "thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone, and microSD storage." An FBI affidavit filed in the Northern District of California included photos of what prosecutors said was a recording device surreptitiously hidden in an executive conference room. Department of Justice The complaint further said that CCTV footage showed Alfozan near the conference room on multiple dates prior to the device's discovery. "According to the complaint, meetings in the executive conference room where Recording Device 1 was discovered frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and business-development opportunities, as well as nonpublic information about OpenAI's technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships," the DOJ said. An FBI affidavit included an image of what prosecutors said is Abdulrahman Alfozan looking behind a television located in the conference room where the recording device was planted. Department of Justice Prosecutors allege that Alfozan used a productivity tool to inquire about OpenAI's building addresses and meeting rooms, and used a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse to submit prompts related to building and hiding an audio recording device. Some of the queries to the productivity agent included a list of "today's meetings in this room" and "what meeting was this presented at and when was it recorded," the complaint said. A screenshot of the criminal complaint shows a list of queries federal prosecutors say Abdulrahman Alfozan made to a "productivity agent." Department of Justice A LinkedIn account with the same name as the defendant in the complaint showed that Alfozan was an engineering lead at OpenAI and is a partner at Raed Ventures, a Riyadh-based venture capital firm that invests in early-stage tech startups across the Middle East and North Africa. A contact associated with the LinkedIn account and a spokesperson for Raed did not immediately return a request for comment. Alfozan's attorney did not return a request for comment. OpenAI said that it found no evidence that the employee improperly accessed or manipulated model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was fired, OpenAI said in the social media post. OpenAI told Business Insider that its models were used to help with the technical investigation of the incident, including analyzing forensic images of the device's storage. It also said it has evidence that the employee intended to plant more recording devices throughout OpenAI's offices. OpenAI said in the X post that the case was an example of how AI can help address " sophisticated security threats ." The announcement comes on the heels of a cluster of firings at OpenAI unrelated to the recording device. In the prior case, the company let go of three safety and alignment employees who it alleged had "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information." The workers, Jasmine Wang, Mikita Balesni, and Tomek Korbak, published a letter disputing some of the claims circulating about their conduct. They wrote that they were concerned about the lack of clarity around their firings, as well as the way they might chill transparency at the company. OpenAI stood by the dismissals. The company published an internal note that said, "Our internal investigation uncovered a significant breach of trust beyond what's outlined in the letter they published and we stand by the decision to not continue their employment." Read the original article on Business Insider
